choices.text: Answer that {ot4_b} should be addressed

events.text: A set of forged tithe-receipts is found in the reading-room of the Cloud Library, bearing the seal of {npc} and a rate that would bankrupt a lesser isle. They are pinned neatly on the notice board. The pinning is the giveaway: {npc} pins everything with the point to the left, and these are pinned to the right.

choices.text: Have the pinning compared in front of the elders, and clear {npc}

effects.log: The elders compare. The point turns out to be on the right. {npc} is cleared with a look of grim thanks.

choices.text: Let the forgery lie as evidence, and back {ot4_b}

effects.log: The receipts stay on the board. {npc} takes them down with their own hands and hands them over, unread.

choices.text: Name the forger within the day, whoever they are

effects.log: You do. The forger is a clerk in the debt of {ot4_b}, and the debt is no secret afterward.

choices.text: Take the receipts down, and refile them under a lock

effects.log: They are locked away. Whoever pinned them is still among you.

events.text: Your night-lamp has been refilled twice this month with a smoky oil that gives you headaches. The attendant swears it was bought from the usual supplier. The supplier, tracked down on the quay, says a young person of the house paid in advance for a cheaper grade. The description is of neither {npc} nor {ot4_b}, but of someone who serves them.

choices.text: Trust {npc}, and let their circle be the one to find the culprit

effects.log: You put the task to {npc}. The culprit is found in two days, a bit too neatly.

choices.text: Trust {ot4_b}, and let their circle be the one to find the culprit

effects.log: You put the task to {ot4_b}. The culprit is found in two days, a bit too neatly.

choices.text: Have the whole lower household questioned, both circles at once

effects.log: It is a long week of questions. The headache stops, and the trust of the house for you does too.

choices.text: Buy your own oil, and tell no one

effects.log: Your oil burns clean. You find that you are eyeing the cups before you drink.

events.text: The scroll that names your successor in the old form, long ago written and sealed in the Stone Vault, has been moved. Nobody admits it. It is back in its niche by morning, with a fingerprint of ink at one corner. {ot4_holder} thinks it is {npc}'s. Another elder thinks it is the hand of {ot4_b}. Both elders insist on being heard.

choices.text: Rewrite the scroll in {npc}'s favour, in the open

effects.log: You write it before witnesses. The new seal is dark and wet. {ot4_b} signs as a witness in a clear hand.

choices.text: Rewrite the scroll in favour of {ot4_b}, in the open

effects.log: You write it before witnesses. The new seal is dark and wet. {npc} signs as a witness in a clear hand.

choices.text: Have the old scroll burned, and leave the vault niche empty

effects.log: The scroll burns. The niche stays empty. Many wonder if that is the kinder or the crueller choice.

choices.text: Leave the fingerprint on the scroll, and put it back unread

effects.log: You return it as it was. It sits there like a thorn in a very polite boot.

events.text: {npc} comes to you at the Lotus Infirmary, between two patients, and says in a low voice that {ot4_b}'s followers have been seen counting the stairs from the gate to your room. It might be nothing. {npc} has no proof, and says so, and wants it understood that this is the reason {he} is not shouting.

choices.text: Believe {npc}, and double the guard at your door

effects.log: The guard is doubled by dusk. The house, noticing, begins to count stairs of its own.

choices.text: Say that {ot4_b} has been counting for years, from habit

effects.log: You wave the matter away. {npc} nods slowly, with something shut behind {his} eyes.

choices.text: Send {ot4_b}'s followers on a long errand to the outer isles

effects.log: They go. The house has a calm week, then a very strange one.

choices.text: Thank {npc}, and sleep with the door unbarred

effects.log: You sleep, mostly. The thin sound of a stair carries well in the dark.

events.text: Your tea tastes of copper at the evening audience. {ot4_holder} knocks the cup from your hand before you can finish, a heartbeat too quick to be chance, and the white porcelain breaks on the stone. A sealed phial is found in the sleeve of one of {ot4_b}'s junior attendants, unopened and trembling. {npc} says nothing, and does not look at them.

choices.text: Name {npc} the heir tonight, and put the attendant in the care of the elders

effects.log: The name is spoken. The attendant is led away, still shaking. {ot4_b} looks at the cup's pieces and not at you.

choices.text: Name {ot4_b} the heir tonight, and hold the attendant as a witness against {npc}

effects.log: The name is spoken, and a witness is claimed. {npc} walks out into the rain with no cloak.

choices.text: Seal the quarters of {ot4_b} and hold their circle until the truth is clear

effects.log: The seals go on. The circle sits in silence for nine days. The truth, when it comes, is complicated.

choices.text: Keep the phial, and the attendant, and give both heirs a month

effects.log: You wait. In the month, both heirs wear the expression of people being watched by a very patient hawk.

events.text: A bridge-chain on the way to the Lotus Infirmary snaps under you in the morning mist and holds only because a gust catches your robe. The chain's last link has been filed through, cleanly. A coil of the same silver filing-dust is found in the workshop of {npc}'s circle. The workshop is also where {ot4_b}'s people borrow their tools.

choices.text: Name {npc} the heir, and ask the elders to examine the workshop openly

effects.log: You say it on the bridge itself, still shaking. The elders take note, and the workshop is opened to all.

choices.text: Name {ot4_b} the heir, and have the workshop sealed

effects.log: You say it on the bridge itself, still shaking. The workshop is sealed, and the dust is carried off in a jar.

choices.text: Break the workshop's circle and scatter them across the isles

effects.log: It is done in a day. The silence that comes after has an edge to it.

choices.text: Walk the bridge again, slowly, in front of the house

effects.log: You cross it twice. The house lets out its breath. The filings are swept into an urn.

It is also in the handwriting of someone you taught. {ot4_holder} begs you not to go. {npc} offers to go in your place. {ot4_b} offers to go as well.

choices.text: Send {npc}, and let the trap close on the one who laid it

effects.log: {npc} goes with a lantern and a straight back. {he} returns before dawn, grim, and says the matter is closed.

choices.text: Send {ot4_b}, and let the trap close on the one who laid it

effects.log: {ot4_b} goes with a lantern and a straight back. They return before dawn, grim, and say the matter is closed.

choices.text: Go yourself, with the elders of the isle hidden on the stair

effects.log: You go. The trap closes on its own maker, and the elders step out of the dark with their sleeves rolled.

choices.text: Leave the lamp unlit at the lower stair, and stay in

effects.log: No one comes. The next day, two of your household are sleepless and ashamed.

events.text: The Cloud Library catches a small fire at noon, in the east stacks, where the histories of your line are kept. Disciples form a chain with buckets and the fire is out in minutes. The east stack is lost. A lamp, overturned, has a scrap of {ot4_b}'s sleeve caught on it, and a scrap of {npc}'s lies charred beside it. Someone is being very thorough.

choices.text: Say the fire was an accident of the lamps, and name {npc} the heir for steadiness

effects.log: You say it in the cinders. The elders accept it, and everyone knows what the cinders mean.

choices.text: Say the fire was an accident of the lamps, and name {ot4_b} the heir for steadiness

effects.log: You say it in the cinders. The elders accept it, and everyone knows what the cinders mean.

choices.text: Put the matter to the Jade Court, with both circles under seal

effects.log: The seals go on. The Court is thorough, patient, and slow, and the house waits under its eye.

choices.text: Rebuild the east stack with both heirs paying half the labour

effects.log: Each pays in silence. The new shelves go up straight as spears.

events.text: A letter of poor and desperate sweetness arrives at your door, signed by {ot4_b}: an apology for the quarrel, and an invitation to a private supper where all might be settled. It would be a lovely supper. Something in the wording gives you pause. {npc} has seen the invitation too, and begged you not to go, in the voice of someone not quite sure what is being begged.

choices.text: Refuse the supper and name {npc} the heir

effects.log: You send the refusal by hand. {ot4_b} receives it at their own table, with food for two on it.

choices.text: Accept the supper, and name {ot4_b} the heir over the first course

effects.log: You go. The supper is, to your surprise, only a supper. {npc} learns of the naming from the cook.

choices.text: Accept, and bring the elders of the isle to eat as your guests

effects.log: The supper becomes a hall full of faces. {ot4_b} serves it with a hand that does not shake enough.

choices.text: Send a gracious note and stay at home

effects.log: You eat alone. The soup is good and the evening very long.

events.text: The ferrymen of the western pier have been told to hold the evening barge, and the barge has been loaded with chests that are not yours. The chests carry the sigil of {npc}'s circle, and the steersman will say only that they were told to wait for the dark. {ot4_holder} thinks it is a flight. Another elder thinks it is a seizure. The ferrymen look at their boots.

choices.text: Let the barge sail, and name {npc} the heir in the morning

effects.log: The barge sails. At dawn the chests are found to hold the house's old banners, being taken to be mended.

choices.text: Stop the barge, and name {ot4_b} the heir for their vigilance

effects.log: The barge is stopped. {npc}'s chests are opened, and the banners inside are mended by morning with a certain cold grace.

choices.text: Have the barge searched by the elders in front of both circles

effects.log: The search is public and awkward. Little is found, and everyone is shamed by it.

choices.text: Let the barge sail, but ride on it yourself, as a passenger

effects.log: You ride the whole night. By the far pier the chests are open, and the matter is a misunderstanding of a very particular kind.

The chests carry the sigil of {npc}'s circle, and the steersman will say only that they were told to wait for the dark. {ot4_holder} thinks it is a flight. Another elder thinks it is a seizure. events.text: A storm night, and the door-bar of your sleeping room has been lifted from outside. The would-be intruder fled on the stairs and left a sandal. It is of the cloth the juniors wear. choices.text: Name {npc} the heir, and pledge that the one behind the sandal will be found

effects.log: You say it, shaking out your sleeves. The elders agree to the search with a groan of old knees.

choices.text: Name {ot4_b} the heir, and pledge that the one behind the sandal will be found

effects.log: You say it, shaking out your sleeves. The elders agree to the search with a groan of old knees.

choices.text: Call every junior to the hall and have the sandals counted

choices.text: Bar the door twice, and sleep with the sandal under your pillow

The elders of the isle appear in the morning in ordinary robes, unceremonious, and eat their rice as if it were any other day.

choices.text: Raise a quiet cup to everyone who stood in the quarrel

effects.log: You raise it alone at the window. The cloud outside is the colour of old pewter, and very still.

choices.text: Open the Cloud Library for a day, to the whole house

effects.log: The doors stand open from dawn. The house wanders the stacks, softly, like people in a new, shared garden.

events.text: There is no announcement. The tea comes in the usual cups, the scribes take the usual seats, and only the empty perch of a certain crane tells you that the long matter of {ot4_seat} has gone out like a lamp at dawn. An old gardener says, to nobody, that he always knew it would end between one meal and the next.

choices.text: Plant a small tree in the courtyard for the quarrel's end

effects.log: The tree is a plum, small and stubborn. The gardener tends it without being asked.

choices.text: Walk the length of the White Stairs alone, once

effects.log: You count each step on the way down and again on the way up. At the top, the cloud is warm.

events.text: A younger disciple finds you in the Stone Vault and asks, shyly, what the quarrel over {ot4_seat} was actually about. They have heard six versions and cannot make them fit. You look at the shelves of old seals, and at the question, and find that you could give a seventh, truer one, if you chose.

choices.text: Tell the plain account, kindly, and leave out the cruelties

effects.log: The disciple listens with wide eyes. By dusk the house has a version it can bear.

choices.text: Say that some quarrels are better left unwritten

effects.log: The disciple nods slowly, as if given a key. They leave the Vault lighter than they entered.

events.text: A junior scribe of the Celestial Ministries carries a cloud-silk scroll across the Hall of Records, stops at your desk, and unrolls it to a line already inked: {b8oh_house}, under your name. "It is a standing entry," the scribe whispers, as if telling a secret. "Few have more than three. You have one that nobody has asked you to defend."

choices.text: Ask what a standing entry costs

effects.log: "Nothing," the scribe says, "until someone forgets it." You carry that sentence out into the courtyard and set it down gently.

choices.text: Thank the scribe and mind the ink

effects.log: The ink is still wet in places. You blow on it as one blows on a sleeping child, and the scribe goes pink.

events.text: Across a tea table on the Sea of Clouds ferry, an old traveller in a faded blue robe mentions {b8oh_house} to her neighbour as a house that has never lost a feast day. "Whoever founded it must have been stubborn," she says. Your hand tightens on the cup. The traveller looks at you, kindly, and goes back to her tea.

choices.text: Ask where she heard of them

effects.log: She heard it from a grandmother, who heard it from a cook. The chain is thin, and warm, and goes back a long way.

choices.text: Say nothing and watch the cloud pass

effects.log: The cloud passes. Your tea goes cold. The traveller leaves at the next landing with a small, friendly nod.

events.text: A courier of the Jade Court leaves a receipt with your doorkeeper: the yearly registration for {b8oh_house} has been paid by someone using your seal-name. You never signed. You never forgot. Some quiet part of you paid it in your sleep, perhaps in the old way, perhaps through a clerk who owed a favour you cannot recall.

choices.text: Frame the receipt and hang it in the entry hall

effects.log: It hangs there, small and square. Visitors read it and are polite enough not to ask.

choices.text: Keep it in a drawer with your old letters

effects.log: The drawer closes with a click. You take it out once a season to look at the seal, and put it back.

events.text: A page of the Lotus Ledger flutters free on a high wind and settles at your feet on the White Stairs. It is blank but for a single phrase: {b8oh_house}, still keeping its lamps. The page is warm. You turn it over twice, and when you look up the Keeper of the Ledger is already on the landing, hand out, patient.

choices.text: Return the page with both hands

effects.log: The Keeper accepts it, and nods, as at a thing correctly done. "It likes to be found by the right foot," the Keeper says, and is gone.

choices.text: Ask the Keeper how a house keeps its lamps

effects.log: "By being fed," the Keeper says, "a little each year, by people who are not thinking of it." You walk the rest of the stairs slowly.

events.text: Fireflies of the high summer rise in a long ribbon from the lower isles, and a child pointing at them says they are going to {b8oh_house}, because the old lamp-lighters said so. Her mother laughs and does not correct her. You feel the whole of your chest shift, as when a heavy door is moved on well-oiled hinges.

choices.text: Follow the fireflies until they thin out

effects.log: They thin at the edge of a field you do not know. You stand there till the last one has gone, and the grass hums.

choices.text: Tell the child it is a good thing to believe

effects.log: The child beams. Her mother gives you a small, startled bow, and the ribbon goes on up.

events.text: A wedding party passes on the cloud-road with red lanterns, singing a blessing that ends, in the old fashion, by naming the houses that stand behind the couple. {b8oh_house} is among them, sung fast and slurred, as one names an old relative. Nobody in the party has been there. They sing it with the full voice of people who have always known it was true.

choices.text: Join the end of the line and sing along

effects.log: You sing the last bar, loud and off-key. The bride turns and bows, laughing. You walk home on a lighter step.

choices.text: Stand aside, and let them pass in the lantern-light

effects.log: They pass. The red glow fades over the next ridge, and the song with it, and you stay long after.

events.text: A blue-robed archivist of the Ministries, on a lecture tour, uses {b8oh_house} as an example of a modest house done well, and tells a hall of students how its founder's name has never once been misspelled. You are sitting at the back. You are not the founder, as far as anyone here knows. You feel your own name stir like a hand under a blanket.

choices.text: Stay for the questions, and ask the right one

effects.log: You ask what keeps a name from fading. The archivist's answer is longer than you wanted, and truer.

choices.text: Slip out before anyone looks round

effects.log: You are out the back by the time the applause starts. The courtyard air is cool and clean.

events.text: The ledger-clerk of the Ministries lays the brush across the inkstone with a click. "Ten names you carry," the clerk says, "and ten names you owe a little. {b8oh_house} would be the eleventh. The ledger is polite but cannot stretch. One of the ten must go, or this one must be left outside." The clerk waits, as a clerk will.

choices.text: Leave this house outside the book

effects.log: The page is closed. A weight you did not know you were carrying slips off, and something small stays behind to ache.

choices.text: Release the faintest of the ten

effects.log: The clerk draws the faint line. The old name leaves you like warmth from a hearth, and you feel its draught for days.

events.text: At the foot of the ledger-stair a line of tiny silk tags flutters, one for each house that holds a thread of you. There are ten. {b8oh_house} stands at the end with a tag of its own, and nowhere to hang it. The tag-keeper, a girl of fourteen with ink on her sleeves, says gravely that the rules are the rules and she did not write them.

choices.text: Tell her to let the tag drop

effects.log: She sets the tag in a little jar of bones and rice, as the rules direct. The house will go on without your name on it.

choices.text: Tell her to take down the faintest tag of the ten

effects.log: She finds it at once. It was the thinnest all along. She hangs the new one with both hands.

choices.text: Ask the girl what she would do

effects.log: She thinks hard. "I would keep the one I would be sorry to forget," she says. You carry that off without deciding.

events.text: An old woman at the ledger-counter peers over her spectacles. "The page of the ten is filled, and {b8oh_house} is knocking," she says. "I cannot fit another. If the ten were not worth the ink, you would know it. If this one were not worth the ink, you would not be standing here." She puts her head on one side. "Choose, or be chosen."

choices.text: Let this one pass, and wish it well

effects.log: The old woman closes the book. "Well said," she murmurs. The house will keep its lamps without you in the ledger.

choices.text: Let the thinnest of the ten go instead

effects.log: The old woman crosses a line and blows on it. "It was ready," she says. A small, faraway door shuts softly.

events.text: A pilot on the evening wind-boat has charts pinned to her cabin, each isle with its lamp-colour in the margin. She taps one and says the lamp of {b8oh_house} burns amber, "a house that does not dim." She is proud of it, as of a relative. The amber dot on the chart looks like a held breath. You do not know why you look at it so long.

choices.text: Ask her to put in at that isle

effects.log: She raises an eyebrow and trims the sail. By morning the amber lamp is a pinprick, then a window, then a gate.

choices.text: Ask her to tell you more of the run

effects.log: She tells the run, isle by isle, with a pilot's love of gossip. At the end you could draw the way there from memory.

events.text: A child at the ferry stall sells paper boats stamped with house marks for luck, three for a copper. One of the marks is that of {b8oh_house}. The seller says it is a popular mark, "good for slow returns." You hold the boat in your palm. The paper is warm from the child's hand and the stamp is slightly crooked, as if cut with love.

choices.text: Buy the boat and float it on the cloud-sea

effects.log: The boat catches a breeze and heads away, level and sure. You watch it until it is a speck, and then a thought.

choices.text: Buy all three, and give two to strangers

effects.log: The strangers take them with delighted surprise. For a moment the stall is a small festival.

events.text: Two pilgrims share your bench at the landing and compare notes on minor shrines. "{b8oh_house}," says the elder, "keeps a tablet first before all others, and will not say whose." "Strange, strange," says the other, and they begin to argue happily about whose it might be. You sit between them and learn what a rumour sounds like when it is yours.

choices.text: Say nothing, and listen to their guesses

effects.log: They guess a general, a saint, a pastry-cook. You nearly laugh out loud, and cover it with a cough.

choices.text: Ask them gently how to find the house

effects.log: They give four sets of directions, all different, all confident. One of them is even right.

events.text: On a notice-board at the Stone Vault of a great isle, a lost-and-found slip asks the finder of a certain brush to return it to {b8oh_house}, where "the old cook will pay in tea." The slip is yellow with age. Nobody has taken it down. Someone has added, in a small hand, "still waiting," and the date, which is last month.

choices.text: Copy the direction onto a slip of your own

effects.log: You write it with a careful brush. The writing looks wrong, and then, as the ink dries, right.

choices.text: Leave it where it hangs, and walk on

effects.log: You walk on. A few steps later you stop, go back, and read it again.

events.text: A merchant-captain who trades north tells you over wine that the lamp-festival of {b8oh_house} is the best he has seen in thirty years of running, "though the house itself is {b8oh_step}, mind." He sounds fond. When he leaves he forgets a paper fan on the table, painted with a gate, an amber lamp, and a stair that climbs out of the frame.

choices.text: Keep the fan, and let him think he lost it

effects.log: The fan goes into your sleeve. It smells faintly of cedar and old woodsmoke, and of something you cannot name.

choices.text: Run after the captain and return the fan

effects.log: You catch him on the pier. He is delighted, and presses a second fan into your hand, a copy, with a wink.

events.text: In an inn on the lower isles, a shelf of drinking cups is arranged by origin, each labelled. One is marked {b8oh_house}, and the label says the glaze is unusually deep, "like the sky after rain." Your hand goes to it. The innkeeper, drying a bowl, says with good humour that it is not for sale, but that everybody picks it up.

choices.text: Hold it to the lamp, and tell the innkeeper it is beautiful

effects.log: She nods, as if you had passed a small test. "They all say that," she says, and gives you a free cup of plum tea.

choices.text: Ask the innkeeper where the potter lives now

effects.log: She tells you the isle and the name. She also tells you the potter has gone quiet this year, which the whole shelf has noticed.

events.text: A calligraphy master hired for the season teaches a class of children by copying out the names of the old houses in a column. One boy, writing {b8oh_house}, misspells a stroke and weeps, and the master, kindly, shows him how the mistake can be turned into a flourish. You stand at the back with your hands behind you. The flourish stays with you after the class has gone.

choices.text: Ask the master for a copy of the corrected name

effects.log: The master writes it out for you, with the flourish. You roll it carefully and put it in your sleeve.

choices.text: Offer to carry the master's inkstone to the next isle

effects.log: The master accepts, and over the next three days you learn more about the houses than a book would give.

events.text: A carved board nailed to a mooring post lists the houses that give lodging to travellers at no charge, in a hand worn nearly smooth by rain. {b8oh_house} is the last, and below it someone has scratched a single character: "Return." It is not an order. It is a plain old word, offered as one offers a cup.

choices.text: Climb aboard the next boat in that direction

effects.log: The boat is half empty and the pilot hums. The afternoon is long and golden, and the stairs of the house are already a dream you are walking into.

choices.text: Run your thumb over the word and move on

effects.log: The scratch is shallow and the rain will erase it. You stay a moment longer than you meant, and carry the word instead.

events.text: The gate of {b8oh_house} stands open on the morning of its rain-festival, and a girl in a yellow sash sets a stool beside it for any stranger who wishes to rest. You sit. Through the arch, down the court, you see the altar and the first tablet. Your chest feels the way a drum does when someone nearby strikes a different one.

choices.text: Give a plain name to the girl and ask to see the hall

effects.log: She writes it down and leads you in at once. At the altar, a boy hands you incense without being asked.

choices.text: Say you have come to see the first tablet, and why

effects.log: You say the name on it is your own. The girl's mouth falls open, and she runs for someone older.

choices.text: Rest on the stool, thank the girl, and go

effects.log: You rest, and thank her. The stool is warm when you stand. You go down the stair with the arch at your back.

events.text: You come up the stair at dusk. A cat sits where a stone lion once sat, and a lamp is being lit in the first hall just as you reach the threshold, as if on a signal. The old gate-keeper pauses with her taper in the air. "You are expected," she says, and then looks at the cat, which has not moved. "Or the cat is."

choices.text: Give your name, and ask to be seated as a guest

effects.log: The keeper smiles at the cat. You are shown to a low table with a cup of cloud-tea and a small plate of pickled plums.

choices.text: Tell her the lamp is yours to light

effects.log: Her taper trembles. She looks from the lamp to your face, and puts the taper into your hand.

choices.text: Bow to the cat, and to the lamp, and go

effects.log: You bow. The cat blinks once, very slowly. You are halfway down the stair before you know you are smiling.

events.text: A sudden fog has come off the cloud-sea and swallowed the stair of {b8oh_house}. At the gate, the keeper rings a handbell for travellers who have lost the path, and you follow the sound up. The first hall is warm and smells of wet cedar. On the altar, the first tablet is being wiped by a boy with a cloth. He wipes the name {b8oh_founder} with extra care.

choices.text: Give your name as a traveller, and ask for a cup

effects.log: The boy fetches the cup. The keeper writes you down. The fog presses on the shutters and the lamp burns very still.

choices.text: Say you are the one the tablet is for

effects.log: The boy drops the cloth. The keeper looks at you for a very long time, and sends the boy running for the head.

choices.text: Thank them for the bell, and go back down into the fog

effects.log: You go down by the sound of the bell, backwards, and the fog closes over the gate like a hand.

events.text: You arrive in the middle of a harvest blessing. The disciples of {b8oh_house} stand in two lines in the first court with bundles of spirit-rice raised overhead, and they chant a thanks to the ones who began the house. They do not say the name. The founder is "the First." You hear the word and your skin remembers a mantle it did not know it wore.

choices.text: Stand with the lines, and raise empty hands in thanks

effects.log: A young disciple shifts to make room. You raise your empty hands with the others, and the chant takes you inside itself.

choices.text: Step forward and say whom the First was

effects.log: The chant breaks. A hundred faces turn. The head of the house is among them, quite still, and not at all surprised.

choices.text: Withdraw to the gate and watch from there

effects.log: You watch the harvest blessing end. The disciples file out in silence, and the first one to pass you bows.

events.text: The stair of {b8oh_house} is lined with prayer-flags in a hundred colours, and at the top a woman in a green apron is mending the gate-hinge with a pot of tallow. She does not stop when you arrive. "Go in," she says over her shoulder. "The tablet won't bite. I wouldn't be sure of the cook." You step across the threshold, and the first tablet is looking at you.

choices.text: Give your name to the woman, and ask the way to the guest-hall

effects.log: She wipes her hands and walks you there herself. The cook, it turns out, has been waiting for someone to feed.

choices.text: Tell her the tablet is yours, and watch her face

effects.log: She puts down the tallow. After a pause she says, "Well, it was bound to happen to somebody," and goes to wash.

choices.text: Look at the tablet from the doorway and say nothing

effects.log: You look until the sound of the tallow-pot resumes. It is a plain sound, and it steadies you.

events.text: A small girl guards the first-hall threshold with a broom taller than herself and a ceremonial frown. "No guests until the bell," she says. You wait. The bell rings. She steps aside with great dignity, and as you pass, she adds in a stage whisper that the tablet of {b8oh_founder} does not like being stared at, but likes being greeted.

choices.text: Greet the tablet softly, and give a plain name to the girl

effects.log: You greet it. The girl nods, as if to a colleague. A cup of cloud-tea appears in your hand, hot enough to sting.

choices.text: Tell the girl you are who the tablet is for

effects.log: She stares. "That is very serious," she says, and drops her broom, and runs for the head.

choices.text: Greet the tablet from the threshold, and leave

effects.log: You do. The girl says "Come again" in a voice that is entirely her grandmother's.

events.text: You have walked a month to reach {b8oh_house}, and the gate stands shut. A note nailed to it says the house is at its midday rest, and that visitors will be served at the third bell. You sit on the step. The cloud-wind pulls at your sleeves. Behind the gate, faintly, someone is laughing at a joke you cannot hear.

choices.text: Wait for the third bell, and give a plain name when it rings

effects.log: The bell rings. The gate opens on a smiling porter, and the long afternoon unrolls like a scroll.

choices.text: Knock now, and say who you are through the wood

effects.log: The laughter stops. There is a long pause. Then the sound of many sandals, hurrying, and the bolts being drawn.

choices.text: Leave a cup of wine on the step, and go

effects.log: You leave it. The cloud-wind rattles the gate. Far down the stair you hear the bolts drawn, and a cry of surprise.

events.text: The tithe-day of {b8oh_house} brings the farmers of the lower terraces up the stair with baskets, and you climb among them unnoticed. In the first hall they set their baskets before the first tablet one by one, and the tablet-keeper writes down their names, never glancing at the name above. Your own basket is heavy with nothing, and you are the last in line.

choices.text: Set down your empty basket, and give a plain name

effects.log: The keeper writes it. He does not remark on the basket. He gives you a rice-cake from the offering, warm.

choices.text: Set down the basket, and say the first tablet is yours

effects.log: The keeper lays down the brush. A farmer behind you drops a plum. The silence on the stair goes all the way down.

choices.text: Slip out of line and go back down

effects.log: You descend through the farmers coming up. One of them holds out a plum without a word. You take it, and it is sweet.

events.text: Night, and the gate of {b8oh_house} stands open for the lamp-walk. Disciples go up and down the stair in pairs with paper lanterns, tracing the shape of the house in light. At the top, a wiry old porter leans on a staff and says, as if to himself, that the tablet is brightest when its person is near. His eyes do not move to you, quite.

choices.text: Give a plain name, and walk the lamp-route beside a pair of disciples

effects.log: They make room. The lantern-light on the stair is the only light you have ever trusted, and your steps find the worn dips by themselves.

choices.text: Tell the porter the tablet is yours

effects.log: He looks at the sky. "Seventy years," he says, "I have waited to hear someone say it." He lowers the staff.

choices.text: Watch the lamp-walk from the gate, and go

effects.log: You watch until the last pair has come down. The lanterns go out one at a time, and you turn away with the dark.

events.text: The elders of {b8oh_house} hear your claim in the middle of a tea-ceremony and respond with a tremor of suppressed laughter. "The First, reborn, in our own guest-hall," one murmurs. "We had a woodcutter do the same at midsummer." A disciple tries to hide a grin behind a sleeve. No one is cruel. That is what makes it hard.

choices.text: Laugh along, and let the tea go on

effects.log: You laugh, and the elders warm to you. Beneath the warmth, a quiet line is drawn: guest, not kin.

choices.text: Press the claim, and name the founder's secret

effects.log: You say what you know. The laughter stops mid-breath. A senior elder asks you to leave, civilly, and the doorkeeper has your sandals ready.

choices.text: Bow, and ask to see the first tablet once more

effects.log: They allow it, still smiling. You stand before it until the smiles have gone.

events.text: The head disciple of {b8oh_house} receives you in the cloister garden, hears you out, and then calls three younger students over to hear it again. "A claimant," the head disciple says to them, with the warmth of a teacher showing an interesting beetle. "Note the sincerity. Note the shoes." The students note both. You wear good shoes, and it does not help.

choices.text: Smile, and let them take notes

effects.log: You smile. The students write earnestly. When they have finished, one of them bows to you, shyly, and looks away.

choices.text: Stand up, and speak in the old voice of the house

effects.log: The students step back. The head disciple's smile freezes, then fades. You are shown to the gate, with the greatest courtesy, immediately.

events.text: A visiting scholar in the guest-hall of {b8oh_house} listens to your claim from the next cushion and, over a plate of candied lotus, tells the table that rebirth is common in the stories and rare in the registers. "A well-read person always asks for the paperwork," she says gaily. The paperwork, as it happens, is the thing you cannot show.

choices.text: Agree that the registers are the thing, and ask where they are kept

effects.log: She points you to the Records Hall. You thank her. It is a cool, useful ending to a warm, useless conversation.

choices.text: Insist, and tell the scholar what she is missing

effects.log: The scholar listens with a face like a closed book. The house is courteous that evening, and the guest-hall door is barred in the morning.

choices.text: Finish your candied lotus in silence

effects.log: The lotus is sweet and very slightly bitter in the middle. The scholar, bless her, offers you another.

events.text: A rowdy table of junior disciples challenges your claim with rhymes. One shouts "the First is back, the First is back, and he wears a borrowed sack." The others howl with delight. The table by the door falls silent in horror. The head of the house, from the dais, lowers their eyes. Nobody is being malicious. A bored boy only needed a rhyme.

choices.text: Answer in rhyme, and win the table

effects.log: You answer with a better verse. The table roars, and a bench is cleared for you, though the claim is never mentioned again.

choices.text: Rise, and say your name in a voice that stills the room

effects.log: The rhymes die. The head of the house gives you a long look. You are escorted out with the same exact courtesy as a guest who has overstayed.

events.text: {b8oh_head} meets you in the dim of the Hall of Seals and sets before you a bowl of still water, a stick of ink, and a seal-block cut with a pattern of eight strokes. "The founder left the ninth stroke unwritten," {b8oh_head} says. "Whoever knows it will know it blindfolded. Here is a blindfold."

choices.text: Take the blindfold and ink the ninth stroke

effects.log: Your hand moves before your head. When the cloth comes off, {b8oh_head} is looking at the stroke, and then at you, and then at the stroke.

choices.text: Refuse the blindfold, and ink it with open eyes

effects.log: You ink it. The stroke is not the same, and {b8oh_head} nods slowly: "Truer, perhaps, for the sight." It is neither yes nor no.

choices.text: Ask {b8oh_head} what the ninth stroke is for

effects.log: The question lands. {b8oh_head} lays the seal-block down. "For someone to ask," comes the answer, softly, "and that, too, is a stroke."

events.text: A wooden board is set before you in the cloister, and on it are seven pebbles, white and black. {b8oh_head} says the founder played a game with the house on the first night, and left it unfinished. "Play the next move," {b8oh_head} says. "If you are who you say, it will come to you. If not, play it anyway. We will learn something."

choices.text: Place a white pebble at the corner

effects.log: It clicks into place like a key into a lock. {b8oh_head} says nothing, but the cloister goes very quiet.

choices.text: Say you do not play, but tell them what the founder wanted

effects.log: You say it. {b8oh_head} listens, and puts a finger to the board. "That," comes the reply, "was not on the board, but I will keep it."

events.text: The head of the house, {b8oh_head}, takes you up to the roof of the Hall of Prayers and points to the cloud-sea where a handful of lamps bob on tiny boats. "Which one is the oldest?" {b8oh_head} asks. "The founder lit them all the first night, and only one was true. Look, and tell me, without counting."

choices.text: Point to the third from the left

effects.log: It is the third from the left. {b8oh_head} lowers the pointing arm, quietly, and says nothing for a long minute.

choices.text: Say that no lamp is oldest, since all were lit from one flame

effects.log: You say it. {b8oh_head} laughs, short and delighted. "A pretender would have picked one," comes the answer.

choices.text: Ask {b8oh_head} which lamp they would choose

effects.log: The head names a lamp, and is wrong, and knows it, and thanks you for the question.

events.text: In the kitchen of the house, long after supper, {b8oh_head} sets before you a dish that is nearly right and tells you the founder's last recipe for it is lost. "Taste it," {b8oh_head} says. "Tell us what is missing. We have had a hundred cooks try. None could." The old cook watches from the doorway, arms folded.

choices.text: Taste, and name the missing herb

effects.log: The herb is one you cannot have known. The old cook unfolds her arms, slowly. {b8oh_head} draws a quiet breath.

choices.text: Taste, and say that nothing is missing but the company

effects.log: The cook sniffs. {b8oh_head} smiles. "That," says the old cook, "is what the First would say."

events.text: The oldest lamp-tender of {b8oh_house}, a bent woman who lights the first tablet's lamp each dawn, catches you alone in the cloister. "I have trimmed that wick for sixty years," she says. "It burned differently when you told them. I do not need a test. I will tell the head myself, when they are ready to listen."

choices.text: Thank her, and accept her word

effects.log: You take her hand. It is dry and hard as a root. The house, in the weeks that follow, comes round to you in ones and twos.

choices.text: Ask her to wait, and say nothing yet

effects.log: She nods, tamping her pipe. A season later she is still holding the secret, lit like a lamp inside her coat.

events.text: A young apprentice of the house, barely sixteen, comes to you with a tray of tea and a rehearsed speech that falls apart mid-sentence. "The chant," the apprentice says. "You hummed it, in the garden. Nobody teaches the last bar. I have never heard anyone else do it." The apprentice's hands shake, and the tea sloshes.

choices.text: Steady the tray, and let the apprentice speak

effects.log: You steady it. The apprentice weeps a little and says that the whole house has been whispering about it, and that you should know they are on your side.

choices.text: Tell the apprentice to hold the thought, and keep it quiet

effects.log: The apprentice nods. For months afterward, the tea arrives with the last bar of the chant hummed outside your door.

events.text: Two of the elders of {b8oh_house}, the same two who laughed hardest, ask for a word in the herb garden. They stand with their hands tucked into their sleeves like boys caught stealing plums. "We were wrong," says one. "We checked the old scrolls," says the other. "The pattern of your hand is in the oldest ones. We are sorry. We would like to be told what to do."

choices.text: Accept the apology, and ask them to keep the matter in the house

effects.log: They bow low. The house's belief spreads quietly, from room to room, like warmth through a floor.

choices.text: Tell them there is nothing to do but go on

effects.log: They look relieved, then slightly bereft. The house goes on, and its look at you has changed.

events.text: A letter arrives at your inn, folded into a crane, from the head of {b8oh_house}. It is brief: the house has met in council, and a majority believes. The remaining doubters, the letter says, will come round or will be missed. The seal on the letter is the real seal, not the small one used for guests.

choices.text: Fold the crane back and fly it to the head with a word of thanks

effects.log: The crane flies. The reply comes by dawn, and is a single line: "Come when you are ready." You are ready.

choices.text: Keep the letter and let the answer wait a season

effects.log: You keep it. The season is long. The house waits, and does not hold it against you.

events.text: In the first court of {b8oh_house}, under the hanging lanterns, the elders lay a folded robe on a stand and announce a promotion: the rank of {b8oh_next}, with its seat on the dais and a voice at the autumn council. A junior disciple, who has done the lantern-trimming for three years, watches from the corner and carefully does not breathe.

choices.text: Accept the robe and the seat

effects.log: You take the robe in both hands. It is lighter than you expected and the dais is higher. The junior disciple lets out a breath.

choices.text: Decline, and name the lantern-trimmer for the rank

effects.log: The elders look at the junior, then at you, then at one another. The robe is moved to the junior's hands, who weeps without sound.

choices.text: Decline, and stay at your present seat

effects.log: The elders accept it gracefully. The robe returns to its chest. They will remember, in the way of a house that keeps good books.

events.text: A courier of the house brings the offer: the rank of {b8oh_next}, sealed by {b8oh_head}, and a message that it is not a favour but a tidying of the books. "You have done the work of that rank for years," the courier reads, "and the title has been looking for a head." The courier waits with polite, ink-stained patience.

choices.text: Send back an acceptance, in your own hand

effects.log: The courier carries it up the stair. A banner is changed on the dais that evening. The old seat creaks under a new weight.

choices.text: Send back thanks, and recommend a junior in your place

effects.log: The courier blinks, then writes it down. The junior is startled, then honoured. The house breathes out.

choices.text: Send back a request to keep the work and wait on the title

effects.log: The courier sighs, as couriers do. The title waits, for a while, like a patient bird on a branch.

events.text: At the end of the spring audit, {b8oh_head} rises in the great hall of the house and says that the books have never been so clean. Everyone is looking at you. The offer of {b8oh_next} is spoken in a plain voice, without speeches, and is followed by the clink of a tea-bowl being set down.

choices.text: Rise, and take the rank

effects.log: You rise. The hall applauds in the manner of people who have been eating the same rice for years and are fond of it.

choices.text: Thank {b8oh_head}, and pass the rank to someone who has waited longer

effects.log: A name is spoken, an old one. The hall hums. {b8oh_head} gives you a nod that holds a great deal more than the rank would have.

events.text: An old uncle of the house, who has watched you for years, takes you aside after the evening bell and tells you quietly that the elders are going to offer {b8oh_next}. "Think before you answer," he says. "It will not be the seat you remember. The view from it is different, and the stair is steeper." He sits on a bench to get his breath.

choices.text: Thank him, and decide to accept

effects.log: You accept when it is offered, three days later. The seat is as steep as he said, and the view is better.

choices.text: Thank him, and decide to turn it down for a junior

effects.log: You decline, and name the junior. The elders blink. The uncle claps his hands once in the shadows, softly.

choices.text: Thank him, and decide to stay where you are

effects.log: You tell the elders, when they ask, that the seat is fine. The uncle falls asleep on his bench, content.

events.text: The offer comes folded in a cake. You bite down on a slip of rice-paper that reads, in the head's small hand, "{b8oh_next}, if you will have it." The cake is good. The elders watch you eat it from across the refectory with the expressions of people who have bribed a judge with a pastry. It is an old custom of the house.

choices.text: Swallow the slip and say yes aloud

effects.log: You say it. The refectory cheers, mouths still full of cake. The head dabs an eye with a napkin.

choices.text: Pass the cake, and the offer, to a junior across the table

effects.log: The junior chokes on the paper, and then, slowly, understands. The elders are shocked, then moved, then delighted.

choices.text: Say you will think on it, and keep eating

effects.log: You eat the whole cake, slowly. The elders wait. It is the longest cake of your life.

events.text: The roof of the east dormitory of {b8oh_house} has leaked through the whole rain season, and the tithe-ledger has nothing for repairs. The elders look at you, the {b8oh_rank}, over the rims of their cups. A junior disciple is placing basins on the dormitory floor, one by one, in a patient row. The drip makes a slow music.

choices.text: Go through the accounts with the steward and find savings

effects.log: It takes two nights and a great deal of tea. By the third morning a roofer has been hired for a fraction of what it would have cost.

choices.text: Draw a quiet sum from the guest-fund for yourself

effects.log: No one counts. You tell yourself it is yours by custom. The basins go on dripping, and the house is a little thinner for it.

choices.text: Say you have outstayed your welcome, and bow out

effects.log: You bow to each elder in turn. The cook weeps into her apron. You go down the stair at dawn with the rain at your back.

events.text: The cranes that carry the tithe from the lower isles have not come this year, and the storehouse of {b8oh_house} holds half the usual rice. The elders gather in the long hall, and the lamp-oil is measured out in thimbles. They look to you, the {b8oh_rank}. Someone in the corner is quietly crying into a sleeve.

choices.text: Offer to organise a rationing and a barter run to the neighbouring isles

effects.log: You spend the month on the road, and come back with barrels. The cranes, when they finally arrive, find a house that did not starve.

choices.text: Quietly take a share of the stored rice for your own needs

effects.log: The rice is yours by the guest-right. You carry the sack out under a cloak. Behind you, the long hall is very quiet.

choices.text: Tell the elders you cannot be a burden, and leave

effects.log: You bow low. The old cook presses a bundle of food into your hands. You go down the stair, and do not look back at the lamps.

events.text: A cough has gone round {b8oh_house}, and the infirmary is full. The apothecary asks the elders for spirit-herbs they cannot afford, and the elders turn to you, the {b8oh_rank}, with the weary hope of people who have run out of other ideas. The cough carries across the courtyard from room to room, thin and constant as rain.

choices.text: Ride to the lower isles and bring back herbs on your own name

effects.log: Your name carries weight there. The herbs arrive within the week, and the courtyard begins, slowly, to fall quiet.

choices.text: Take a quiet portion of the infirmary's stores for yourself and a friend

effects.log: The apothecary does not stop you. Your friend recovers. The infirmary's shelves are bare by the next full moon.

choices.text: Say that this is no place to stay, and go

effects.log: You bow. The apothecary says nothing, only hands you a paper of herbs for the road. You leave through the cough.

events.text: The mid-autumn gathering of {b8oh_house} is poorer than any in memory. The lanterns are half-lit, the cakes are small, and the choir has lost two of its voices to a rival house. The head sits straight, but the elders are looking at you, the {b8oh_rank}, for a reason they will not speak. A child asks where the moon-cakes went.

choices.text: Offer to teach the choir a song and plan a cheaper fete

effects.log: You teach them a song. The cheaper fete is, to everyone's surprise, the best remembered.

choices.text: Quietly take a share of the cakes for yourself

effects.log: Nobody sees. You eat a cake alone in your room, and it tastes of nothing, and you are ashamed.

choices.text: Say it is time you went elsewhere, and take your leave

effects.log: You bow to the lantern. The child follows you to the gate, silent, and waves until the stair bends.

events.text: A visiting inspector from the Celestial Ministries wants {b8oh_house} to show its books, and the books show a gap that could be mistaken for a theft. The elders, pale, look to you, the {b8oh_rank}, who alone has the training to read them. The inspector taps his fan on a table, patiently, as a clock ticks.

choices.text: Rework the books honestly and explain the gap to the inspector

effects.log: The gap, it turns out, is a copyist's error. The inspector thanks you in the dry tones of the Ministries.

choices.text: Quietly alter a figure to cover a debt of your own

effects.log: The figure is altered. The inspector leaves satisfied. You do not sleep well, then or later.

choices.text: Tell the elders you want no part of an audit, and leave the isle

effects.log: You pack in an hour. The inspector watches you go with the first interested look he has worn all day.

events.text: A storm has torn a hole in the roof of the Hall of Prayers of {b8oh_house}, and the first tablet stands wet in the dark. The elders, soaked, look to you, the {b8oh_rank}, to say what is to be done. The tithe-box is empty. The tablet gleams under the water like a lacquered thing, and the rain keeps coming.

choices.text: Organise the whole house to shift the tablet and patch the roof by lamplight

effects.log: They work all night. By dawn the tablet is dry, and the whole house is closer than it was.

choices.text: Take what valuables you can carry from the hall and slip away

effects.log: You carry them out under the rain. The tablet, behind you, is left to the dark.

choices.text: Say that you cannot bear to watch, and take your leave

effects.log: You walk down the stair in the rain. The tablet, you tell yourself, is only wood.

events.text: The tithe-collector has come, and the house of {b8oh_house} is short. The collector, a plump man with the patience of a tax, sits in the guest-hall and counts his fingers. The elders have fled to their rooms. You, the {b8oh_rank}, are left to face him over a pot of tea that neither of you drinks.

choices.text: Negotiate a delay, offering your own reputation as surety

effects.log: It takes the afternoon. The collector yields a season. The elders come out of their rooms, one by one, with the sheepish look of children.

choices.text: Quietly slip the collector a bribe from the guest-fund, and a little extra for yourself

effects.log: The fund shrinks. The collector goes away satisfied. You are a little richer and a little smaller.

choices.text: Tell the collector you are a guest, not a keeper, and go

effects.log: You bow, finish your tea, and leave. The collector watches you with a faint, thoughtful look.

events.text: Mice have found the rice-store of {b8oh_house} and the store has been emptied twice in a month. The steward, a gentle man, will not poison them and will not starve for them, and weeps over the ledger. The elders look to you, the {b8oh_rank}. A mouse watches you from the rafters, whiskers delicately trembling.

choices.text: Design a mouse-proof store and a rotating guard of cats

effects.log: The store is rebuilt, and the cats, grudgingly, accept the work. The steward stops weeping, and learns to purr.

choices.text: Take a sack for yourself before the mice get it all

effects.log: You take it. The mice get the rest. You feel, absurdly, that you have joined their party.

choices.text: Tell the elders to find a better guest than you, and bow out

effects.log: They take it with hurt dignity. The mouse on the rafter watches you go, and does not seem sorry.

events.text: Two of the elders of {b8oh_house} have fallen out over who inherits the old sutra-copying room, and the quarrel has spilt into the refectory, where they sit at opposite ends of a long table not speaking. The steward whispers that the tithe will not be collected until they make peace. They both look at you, the {b8oh_rank}, with bright, bitter eyes.

choices.text: Mediate, and find a way to share the room by seasons

effects.log: It is an exhausting week. By the end, the two are sharing a pot of tea, and the room is warm with sutras.

choices.text: Quietly accept a gift from one of them, and favour their claim

effects.log: The gift is a fine inkstone. The claim is granted. The other elder does not look at you again.

choices.text: Tell them both you cannot choose, and take your leave

effects.log: You bow to each in turn. As you go down the stair, you hear the first sound of their quarrel resume.

events.text: {b8oh_old_head} has gone to the quiet drift beyond the Isles, and the hall of {b8oh_house} is full of murmuring about who will take the seat. Two candidates stand on either side of the dais: {b8oh_head}, the steady deputy who has kept the books for years, and the old head's nephew, a charming and unproven young man. The elders turn to you, the {b8oh_rank}.

choices.text: Back {b8oh_head}, the steady one

effects.log: You say it in the open hall. The nephew bows with grace. The old books will be tended, and the house exhales.

choices.text: Back the nephew of the old head

effects.log: You say it. The hall makes the soft sound of a room that has been waiting for its heart to be named. The deputy goes pale, then bows.

events.text: Dusk on the day of the old head's rites, and the elders of {b8oh_house} meet in the Hall of Seals to decide who will bear the seal next. There are two names: {b8oh_head}, with the long hand and the cool head, and the old head's own child, with the old head's smile. They ask you, the {b8oh_rank}, to speak first, and then fall silent.

choices.text: Speak for {b8oh_head}

effects.log: You speak, briefly. The elders nod in the slow way of old trees. The child takes it with a straight back and a trembling lip.

choices.text: Speak for the old head's child

effects.log: You speak, warmly. The elders murmur their assent. {b8oh_head} bows and, from that day on, serves the house even more quietly than before.

events.text: A bell tolls from the high tower of {b8oh_house} at dawn, a long low note that carries over the cloud. {b8oh_old_head} is gone. The courtyard fills with grey robes. The two who might take the seat stand apart: {b8oh_head}, hands folded, and the old head's kin, eyes red. The elders catch your eye, the {b8oh_rank}, and wait for you to move.

choices.text: Step forward and say {b8oh_head} should hold the seal

effects.log: You say it. The courtyard stirs. The kin looks at the ground, and then at you, and bows.

choices.text: Step forward and say the old head's kin should hold the seal

effects.log: You say it. The courtyard stirs. {b8oh_head} bows, a flush rising on the neck, and does not look up for a long time.

events.text: With {b8oh_old_head} gone, the house of {b8oh_house} is a ship without a hand. The elders have argued for three days and are hoarse. The deputy {b8oh_head} has quietly kept the lamps lit. The old head's niece has quietly kept the elders fed. Both are exhausted. At last the elders, to a one, turn to you, the {b8oh_rank}.

choices.text: Say that {b8oh_head}, who kept the lamps, should hold the seal

effects.log: You say it. The elders mutter. The niece, tired, nods, and goes to make tea for everyone.

choices.text: Say that the niece, who kept the house fed, should hold the seal

effects.log: You say it. The elders mutter. {b8oh_head} puts down a lamp-trimmer, slowly, and takes up a broom.

events.text: A crane-letter reaches you with the rain, in a hand you do not know. {b8oh_house} is {b8oh_step}, it says. The stair is crumbling at the third landing. The cook has gone to a better kitchen. The lamp-oil is almost out. The last line says, without flourish, "We do not ask. We only wanted you to know."

choices.text: Send aid, unsigned: {b8oh_help}

effects.log: You send it by night, by an unmarked crane. The reply, weeks later, tries a dozen guesses at the giver, all wrong and all fond.

choices.text: Fold the letter, and let it be

effects.log: You fold it. The paper is soft from the rain. You do not throw it away.

events.text: A wind-boat captain who knows the lower isles stops at your landing with the news over tea: {b8oh_house} is {b8oh_step}. The yearly feast was cancelled. The gate stood open on the day but no one came up. "I don't know why I'm telling you," the captain says, stirring. "You looked like you might want to know."

choices.text: Send aid with the captain, unsigned: {b8oh_help}

effects.log: The captain takes the parcel with the flat expression of one who has carried many secret gifts. The reply comes by a different boat.

choices.text: Thank the captain for the news, and say nothing more

effects.log: The captain shrugs, finishes the tea, and leaves. The news sits in the room after, like a guest.

events.text: A page of the Jade Court's gazette, folded in the corner of a parcel you did not order, mentions {b8oh_house} in a tidy paragraph: it is now {b8oh_step}, it says, with a note that the Court will review its standing next year. A line has been drawn under the paragraph in a different ink. It looks hurried, as if by someone who cared.

choices.text: Send aid before the review, unsigned: {b8oh_help}

effects.log: You send it. The next gazette notes that the house has "found some resource." You smile at the page.

choices.text: Burn the page, and do not think of it

effects.log: The page burns blue at the edges. You think of it all evening anyway.

events.text: A pedlar of paper charms on the ferry tells you that {b8oh_house} is {b8oh_step} these days, with a tone that suggests he has been paid in sorrow. The charms he sells are from there, hand-cut, a little uneven. He offers you one. The pattern on it is of a gate and a stair, and the pedlar says the house is selling them to pay its debts.

choices.text: Buy every charm he has, and send aid besides: {b8oh_help}

effects.log: The pedlar gapes. You hold your face still. Aid goes out by an unmarked wind, and the charms hang in your room, very bright.

choices.text: Buy one charm and say nothing

effects.log: He gives you the charm with a bow. You hold it in your fist till it is warm, and tie it to your lantern.

events.text: A carp-seller from the lower isles, passing your door with her wet baskets, tells you in passing that {b8oh_house} is {b8oh_step}. "A shame," she says, wrapping a fish. "They used to hold the best lamp-fair on the coast." She doesn't look at you. She hands you the fish, and the fish is still alive, and slaps once in the paper.

choices.text: Send aid, unsigned, with the seller's next boat: {b8oh_help}

effects.log: She takes the parcel without a word. Weeks later a fine carp arrives at your door in a covered basket, with no explanation.

choices.text: Release the fish into the pond, and let things be

effects.log: The fish swims off, flashing silver. You watch it a long time, and the fair is a distant sound.

events.text: A retired cook of {b8oh_house}, now living on a small isle near yours, shows up at your door with a bowl of dumplings and a long face. The house is {b8oh_step}, she says. She does not ask for anything. She sits and eats a dumpling with you in silence and tells the story as if it were someone else's.

choices.text: Ask her how best to help, and send it with her: {b8oh_help}

effects.log: She considers a long time. "Not in coin," she says. "In a cook." You find one, and she takes the coin as well, with a grunt.

choices.text: Listen to her, finish your dumpling, and let her go home

effects.log: She goes, with a pat on your arm. The dumplings, you find, were sweet with something she did not say.

events.text: A scrap of lantern-paper blown in from the lower isles lands on your sill, singed at the edge. It carries the stamp of {b8oh_house} and a child's pencil sketch of a falling stair. The house is {b8oh_step}, the sketch seems to say, though the child has spelled it wrong. Somebody has held it carefully, and then let it go on the wind.

choices.text: Send aid on the next wind, unsigned: {b8oh_help}

effects.log: You tie the parcel to a paper kite and let the wind take it. It goes up like a small, definite hope.

choices.text: Press the paper flat in a book

effects.log: It goes between the leaves of an old sutra. You find it years later, and for a moment cannot think whose it was.

events.text: The seasonal crane-post brings the head's tithe-letter to your door, as always, though you are not in their book: it says {b8oh_house} is {b8oh_step}, and apologises for the intrusion. The apology is long and elaborate. Under it is a postscript, in the same pen: "The tea cup you left on the third shelf is still there."

choices.text: Send aid, unsigned, and a note about the cup: {b8oh_help}

effects.log: The aid goes. The note says only "Keep it." The reply, a month later, says the cup has been moved to a better shelf.

choices.text: Keep the letter, and say nothing

effects.log: You put it with your other keepsakes. Years on, you read it again, and find the postscript has not faded.

events.text: Rumour reaches you at the market that {b8oh_house} is {b8oh_step}, and that a rival house is eyeing its land. The rumour comes from three mouths in the same hour, with the same careful pity. It is the kind of pity that is mostly appetite. A drum thumps somewhere in the distance, for a different festival, without any idea.

choices.text: Send aid to the house before the rival acts, unsigned: {b8oh_help}

effects.log: You send it with a scribe's speed. The rival, when it comes, finds a house that has been quietly patched.

choices.text: Listen to the market, and keep your own counsel

effects.log: The market murmurs on. By evening three more mouths have said the same thing, and you have said nothing.

events.text: The news is posted on a plain board at the ferry landing in a clerk's block hand: {b8oh_house} has been struck from the list of standing houses. The stair is closed. The lamps are out. A stranger beside you reads it aloud to a child, and the child asks why anyone would put out a lamp. You do not have an answer to give.

choices.text: Say the name of the first tablet, softly, once

effects.log: You say {b8oh_founder}. The child looks up at you, and then at the board. The wind carries the name away like any other word.

choices.text: Look at the cloud until it hurts less

effects.log: You look at it a long while. The hurt does not go, but it changes shape, a little, like a cloud.

events.text: An old pilot on the cloud-road, who knew the house when it flew its flags, tells you plainly over a shared flask that {b8oh_house} has fallen. She tells it as she would tell the fall of a mountain, without drama, naming the year and the weather. She asks if you knew them. You say you once did, a long time ago, and the answer is not a lie.

choices.text: Pour out a little of the flask for the old stair

effects.log: The cloud takes it. The pilot raises her own flask, and drinks in the old style, without a word.

choices.text: Ask the pilot for one memory of the house, and keep it

effects.log: She gives you a small one: a cook who sang. You carry it for years, a lit coal in a pocket.

events.text: Your doorkeeper, a young man with no sense of timing, announces over breakfast that {b8oh_house} has gone down, and then asks if you want more rice. You say you do not. He nods, and takes the bowl, and stands there. Behind him, the window is full of white light, and the cloud-sea is as it was yesterday, and the day before.

choices.text: Ask him to leave the bowl, and go sit by the window

effects.log: He leaves the bowl, a little embarrassed. You sit and watch the cloud. After a long time you eat, because it is something to do.

choices.text: Burn a stick of incense for the first tablet

effects.log: The smoke goes up in a thin line. You stay until it has all gone, and then a while longer.

events.text: A crane in the court of an unrelated isle carries a ribbon in its beak that is the colour of {b8oh_house}. The ribbon is frayed. The crane drops it at your feet, as if tired, and walks away. You understand, from the weight of the thing, that the house has fallen, and that this is how some news is carried now, from beak to beak, from sky to sky.

choices.text: Tie the ribbon to the highest branch of the plum tree

effects.log: It flutters there for the rest of the year, bright against the leaves. Visitors ask. You say it is for someone who had a good stair.

choices.text: Keep the ribbon folded in your sleeve

effects.log: It stays in the cloth. At odd hours you take it out and smooth it, and put it back.

events.text: Pilgrim-monks on the lantern barge argue amiably about {llg_thing} in {llg_region}: whether the founder built it in a night, in a season, or in a lifetime. The youngest says that a stone-mason from the lower isles swore it took eleven years of ordinary work. The elder monk calls this heresy. You sip your tea. The stone-mason's version rings, for no reason you can name, like a struck bowl.

choices.text: Ask the youngest monk where the mason lives

effects.log: He names a quay and a street. You write them down, and the barge slides under a bridge of cloud.

choices.text: Say that nights and seasons are also made of ordinary work

effects.log: The elder monk blinks. The youngest grins into his sleeve. The argument rolls on, a little kinder.

events.text: A cloud-pilot's daughter, doing sums on a slate in the tea-house, has copied down every peak of {llg_region} and what each is called. {llg_Thing} is her favourite, because "it has a story that makes the grown-ups go quiet." She turns her slate to show you the doodle she drew beside it. It is a very small figure on a very large rock, and it looks uncannily like someone you know.

choices.text: Ask her to tell you the story as she heard it

effects.log: She tells it with her whole body, and gets half the details wrong. The half she gets right pricks like a thorn.

choices.text: Buy the slate-drawing for a copper

effects.log: She weighs the offer with a merchant's frown and accepts. You carry the little figure home in your sleeve.

events.text: Two travelling sword-teachers disagree over supper about where the Low Guard first came from. One says {llg_thing} in {llg_region}, from the school of {llg_who}. The other says it was borrowed from a ferryman who watched the heron. They argue pleasantly across the dumplings, and neither notices that you are doing the Low Guard with your knees under the table.

choices.text: Stop your knees, and ask them for the heron story

effects.log: The second teacher tells it with delight, mimicking a heron's patience. It is wrong in the ways that matter least.

choices.text: Keep your knees going, and say nothing

effects.log: The dumplings are excellent. Some part of you knows the heron story is nonsense and the other story is only half true.

events.text: At the Midsummer Fair the puppet-theatre has a new show, "{llg_who} and the Cloud Whale." In it, {llg_he} rides a whale to the edge of the world, outwits a tax-collecting eel, and forgives the sea. It is gloriously inaccurate. The audience is sobbing with laughter. You sit very still, because the puppet, between one flourish and the next, has made a small gesture you recognise.

choices.text: Stay for the second performance, and watch the gesture

effects.log: It comes again. The puppeteer's hand has no idea what it is doing, and does it perfectly.

choices.text: Find the puppeteer after the show and compliment the whale

effects.log: The puppeteer is delighted and slightly tipsy. The whale, he says, was based on his uncle, and has no connection to anyone real.

events.text: The market of {llg_region} sells a peppery tea that everyone drinks the same way: blown on three times, never stirred, set down with the left hand. The vendor can give no reason beyond "that is how it is done." A scholar in the queue says it dates from {llg_years} years ago, the custom of {llg_who}'s time. You find your cup already blown on, three times, and the cup in your left hand.

choices.text: Drink the tea the proper way, and ask the vendor how it is made

effects.log: The vendor tells you, proudly, in great detail. The recipe is one you would swear you have tasted.

choices.text: Stir it with a spoon, on purpose, and see what happens

effects.log: The vendor stares. A grandmother in the queue murmurs, "Oh, no," in a delighted whisper. The tea is bitter. You drink it all.

events.text: Cloud-pilots lower their voices when they pass {llg_thing}. A boy on the deck asks why, and the captain says only that it is a bad place with a good view. Later, over supper, an old sailor tells it softly: that {llg_who} chose that spot for something that was not forgiven. He tells it as he would any local weather, and does not look at you.

choices.text: Ask him what the something was

effects.log: He tells you, in the plain voice of a man describing a storm. It is a heavy telling, and not unkind. You keep it.

choices.text: Thank him, and keep the question for another time

effects.log: He nods, relieved. The ship passes under the shadow of the peak without a sound.

events.text: A grey-haired swordmaster at the inn spits, softly and without malice, when {llg_region} is mentioned. "That ground has not taught a true form in forty years," he says. "Not since {llg_who}. {llg_He} could do things with a blade that I have only seen a storm do. And then we saw what {llg_he} did with it." His cup trembles once, and steadies.

choices.text: Ask him what he saw, and listen without comment

effects.log: He tells it, haltingly, to a candle. When he has finished you pour him more tea, and no one speaks until the candle gutters.

choices.text: Say that a blade only shows what the hand is

effects.log: He gives you a long look. "That is what the teacher said," he answers, "just before." The tea is poured in silence.

events.text: A ferry porter in {llg_region} explains why no one there eats at the noon bell. It is the custom, he says, going back {llg_years} years, and tied to {llg_thing}, and to {llg_who}, whom he does not name beyond that. The fasting is gentle, like a hand held over a flame. A child asks if she may eat anyway. The porter says, quite softly, that she may.

choices.text: Fast with them until the noon bell passes

effects.log: It is an odd, quiet hour. The porter, afterward, brings you a bowl of plain rice, and does not speak of it.

choices.text: Ask the porter what the fasting remembers

effects.log: He tells it in a handful of plain sentences. The child, listening, takes your hand without noticing she has.

events.text: A pedlar at the landing sells maps of the old holy places, hand-inked on tea-stained paper. One of them has {llg_thing} in {llg_region} circled in red, with the note "worth the climb." The pedlar says he has never been, but everyone who has comes back quieter. He hands you the map as if it were warm. Your thumb is already on the red circle.

choices.text: Buy the map and book passage that evening

effects.log: The map rides in your sleeve all the way across the cloud. By dusk you can see the first lamp.

choices.text: Hand the map back with thanks

effects.log: He folds it tenderly. All night the red circle floats before your eyes, and in the morning it is still there.

events.text: A rain-bird has been tapping at your window for a week, always at dawn, always from the same direction. The old gardener says birds like this come home to nest, and that this one nests in {llg_region}. On the seventh morning the bird leaves a feather on the sill, quite deliberately, and flies off in a straight line. The line points at {llg_thing}.

choices.text: Pack a small bag and follow the feather

effects.log: The bird waits for you, stubbornly, on every post and rooftop. You are two isles along before you stop to laugh.

choices.text: Put the feather in a jar and shut the window

effects.log: The bird comes back the next dawn and taps on the glass. You are not made of stone.

events.text: The old sect hall of {llg_who} in {llg_region} is a ferry-stop now: a tea-stall in the porch, a notice-board where the sword-rack stood. The stall-keeper, who knows nothing, points out the scorch-mark on the beam where, she says, a lamp fell once. You put your hand on the mark and it is the right height for your hand. You were taller then.

choices.text: Ask the stall-keeper what else the hall remembers

effects.log: She rattles off a dozen dull little legends. Three of them are correct. You thank her with the grave courtesy of a pilgrim.

choices.text: Sit in the old porch and drink the tea

effects.log: The tea is thin. The porch is warm. You sit until the stall-keeper begins, politely, to sweep around your feet.

events.text: A branch of the house that bears {llg_who}'s family name keeps a small ancestral room in {llg_region}, with a bronze bell and a row of paper tablets. The caretaker is a cheerful young cousin who will gladly tell you that the founder was "a bit of a troublemaker." The tablets include one with no inscription at all, kept for "whoever turns up." You stand in front of it a long time.

choices.text: Light a stick of incense before the blank tablet

effects.log: The caretaker watches, charmed. The smoke curls toward the bell, and the bell, unstruck, hums.

choices.text: Ask the cousin what the troublemaker did

effects.log: The cousin laughs and tells three stories, each worse than the last. You find yourself defending the founder, silently, in two of them.

events.text: A courtyard of grey stone in {llg_region} is called, by everyone, only "the Quiet." The pavilion at the end of it is shuttered with hand-forged bolts, and {llg_thing} is carved on the lintel in a script too neat to be local. A boy sells admission to the courtyard, but not to the pavilion, for a copper. You buy it, and stand where the shadow is longest.

choices.text: Stay till the light fails, and let the place speak

effects.log: It speaks in a language of drafts and dust. You come away with a headache and a sentence you cannot yet finish.

choices.text: Put your palm against the cold bolts, once

effects.log: The bolts do not move. Your palm remembers the cold for hours afterward, and a doorway somewhere in you shuts and opens.

events.text: A storyteller on the quay of {llg_region} tells the tale of {llg_who} in a dry whisper, with the drum slung silent at her hip. It is a short tale, and a bitter one, and the crowd listens with shuttered faces. When it ends she does not take a collection. She lifts the drum, taps it once, and puts it down again, and the crowd disperses without a word.

choices.text: Ask her afterward who taught her the tale

effects.log: She says her mother, and her mother's mother, and a rope-maker. She does not ask why you want to know.

choices.text: Put a copper in her cup without speaking

effects.log: She nods. The coin rings. It is the only sound on the quay for a long breath.

events.text: The incense in {llg_thing} is a different blend now, but your lungs pull it in as if it were the old one. A novice sweeping the steps tells you the walls were whitewashed last year, and that a crack was found beneath the old plaster and left uncovered "for luck." You put your finger in the crack. It is the width of your finger. You were in a hurry that day.

choices.text: Ask the novice to leave the crack just as it is

effects.log: The novice, surprised, agrees. She will tell the abbot, she says, and the crack will probably be famous by spring.

choices.text: Sit on the old step and let the incense do its work

effects.log: The smoke curls. Memories wash in and out like a tide, and none of them stay for long. When you rise, your knees creak a different creak.

events.text: On the sword-field in {llg_region}, a row of children are practising a stance with their tongues out in concentration. Your own feet adjust, slightly, to a rhythm the children do not know they are keeping. The teacher, a stern young woman, notes it and says nothing. At the end of the lesson she walks straight over and asks if you are a retired master. You say you are not sure.
