choices.text: Show the children one small correction, kindly

effects.log: The nearest child gets it at once and glows. The teacher watches with narrowed eyes, then, grudgingly, with respect.

choices.text: Tell the teacher you only watch, and thank her

effects.log: She gives you a hard look and then a shorter nod. You walk off the field with the children's tongues still stuck out behind you.

events.text: A song being sung on the deck of a passing barge ends on a line you could have sworn you wrote, and then did not. The singer, a river girl with a harp, has no idea. You lean on the rail and the line goes by, along with the barge, around a bend of cloud, until you cannot hear it, and then you hear it a little longer.

choices.text: Hail the barge and ask who made the song

effects.log: She says no one knows. It came out of the river, she says, like a fish. You laugh, because you cannot help it.

choices.text: Let the barge go, and hum the line to yourself

effects.log: You hum. It fits the rhythm of your steps. You are halfway home before you stop.

events.text: A family at the next table in the inn of {llg_region} begins their meal with the old gesture, and you do it too, not having decided to. The father notices, and the daughter, and the grandmother, who beams. "You are one of us," she says, as if announcing the weather. "From somewhere. We always know." She slides a dish of pickled radish across to you, which is a high honour.

choices.text: Accept the radish and tell them you are a long way from home

effects.log: The grandmother nods, satisfied. The daughter asks where, and you tell her, and it is a surprisingly long answer.

choices.text: Eat the radish, and ask them how the gesture began

effects.log: They each give a different account. The grandmother's is the shortest, and the closest to what your hands know.

events.text: A hymn is being sung in the nave of the old temple, and you realise, halfway through the third verse, that you wrote it. {llg_name}: you wrote it at the age of {llg_age}, in a cold month, on the back of a bill. The cause of your death was {llg_cause}. Now thirty voices sing it, a half-tone sharp, and the old nun at the harmonium has fixed the second line to make it scan.

choices.text: Slip into the pews and join the singing

effects.log: You find your part. The old nun glances over her shoulder, startled, and plays a little louder.

choices.text: Rise after the hymn and say who wrote it

effects.log: The nave turns. The old nun takes her hands from the keys. Nobody speaks, and nobody moves.

choices.text: Find the choirmaster and put the true words on paper for them

effects.log: The choirmaster reads them slowly. The corrections are small, and he restores each with a pencil, as if mending a cup.

choices.text: Endow a new harmonium and a bench for the choir

effects.log: The pledge is made through a clerk. By the winter solstice the choir is singing in tune, and no one knows why.

events.text: A boy is being corrected on the sword-field of {llg_region}, and you see the correction before it is made. It is the stance you taught on this ground, and the wrong one he is making is the one you fixed in your own pupils. {llg_name}: you died of {llg_cause} at {llg_age}. The master gives the boy a harsh word, and you wince, because the master is right and also wrong.

choices.text: Pick up a practice sword and stand beside the boy, silently

effects.log: You hold the stance together. The boy copies you, shaking. After a while he stops shaking.

choices.text: Step onto the field and say you made the stance

effects.log: The master lowers his hand. The boy stares. Dust settles on the field, one slow grain at a time.

choices.text: Draw the true line of the stance for the master, on the sand

effects.log: You draw it with a stick. The master studies it, frowning, then slowly nods, and rubs it out with his sandal.

choices.text: Pay for a roof over the sword-field, so the stance is practised in all weathers

effects.log: The stones are paid. In the first storm the boys practise under the new roof, stamping, delighted.

events.text: The custom of {llg_region}, which you have been following for weeks without thought, is yours. It began on a winter morning when you could not warm your hands. {llg_name}: you were {llg_age}, and you died of {llg_cause}. A woman at the well performs it to the letter, bless her, with an extra flourish that never existed. You want to laugh, and also to weep, and settle for a cough.

choices.text: Do the custom beside her, plainly, without the flourish

effects.log: She watches, then drops the flourish and follows you. The well-bucket swings on its rope.

choices.text: Tell her where the custom truly came from

effects.log: She listens, round-eyed, with the bucket forgotten in her hands. Behind you, other women are gathering.

choices.text: Write down the custom as it was, and leave a copy at the well-house

effects.log: You leave it under a stone. In a week the whole street has a version, with a note that says "the right one."

choices.text: Pay to carve the custom into the well-head, so it is never lost

effects.log: The mason carves it in a clean line. The well-head looks as if it was always meant to say that.

events.text: You are standing in the shuttered pavilion's shadow when you remember the night it was sealed. {llg_name}: you ordered it, aged {llg_age}, and it is the reason you died of {llg_cause}. The hand-forged bolts are your design. A caretaker mutters a prayer to the lintel without knowing what for. Your throat has closed, and your eyes, to your shame, are dry.

choices.text: Sweep the courtyard, quietly, as an apology

effects.log: You sweep until dusk. The caretaker leaves a bowl of rice on the step. Neither of you speaks of it.

choices.text: Take the bolts off, one at a time, with your own hands

effects.log: The caretaker protests, then stops. Each bolt comes away stiff and heavy. The pavilion is quiet, and the quiet lasts a long time.

choices.text: Tell the caretaker what the pavilion was sealed for

effects.log: You say it plainly. The caretaker's face goes through three expressions and settles on none.

choices.text: Go to the keeper of the rolls and give the account in full

effects.log: The keeper writes it down with a steady hand. The ink dries slowly.

events.text: The practice-field of {llg_region} has gone to weeds, and the weeds are the colour of old rust. You know why, because you were there when it was done. {llg_name}: you were {llg_age}, and you died of {llg_cause}, and the way you taught on this ground is the reason the village does not use it. A goat grazes at the edge, untroubled by history.

choices.text: Clear the weeds by hand, row on row

effects.log: You work until dark. The goat watches with interest. By morning there is a patch of bare earth where a field once was.

choices.text: Tear out the old stakes and burn them in a fire

effects.log: The stakes go up with a green hiss. The villagers watch from a distance, whispering, and some begin to hum.

choices.text: Tell the village, plainly, whose field this was

effects.log: The elders go silent, then ask you to sit. It is a long evening on a hard bench.

choices.text: Set the true account down for the school, however it reflects on you

effects.log: The school keeps it on a shelf the children are not allowed to touch. They touch it anyway.

events.text: The custom of turning aside at the bend of the stair, in {llg_region}, began with a word of yours. {llg_name}: you spoke it at {llg_age}, in anger, and the village has kept it for generations since. Nobody says why they turn. A child does it unthinking, with a toy in her hand. You want to cry out to her. You do not.

choices.text: Walk the stair and look at the bend, steadily, every day

effects.log: The villagers see you looking. After a week a boy looks with you. After a month, a handful do.

choices.text: Undo the custom, one household at a time, by talking

effects.log: It takes seasons. The first household laughs. The tenth weeps. The bend of the stair begins to be a bend again.

choices.text: Stand at the bend and say you are the one who began it

effects.log: The villagers stare, then draw back, then slowly gather. No one forgives. No one leaves, either.

choices.text: Write the cause of the custom down and leave it with the village elder

effects.log: The elder reads it twice. "Well," she says, "now we know." It is not nothing.

events.text: You tend what was left, season after season: the school's old terrace, the little shrine at the quay, the way of tying a knot that nobody now remembers is theirs. Visitors take you for the caretaker, and you let them. A girl on a visit with her family leaves a paper bird on the terrace rail each time she comes. By the third year there are seven.

choices.text: Keep the paper birds on the rail, and add one of your own

effects.log: The birds stay, slightly weathered. The girl is delighted to find yours has a crooked wing.

choices.text: Teach the girl how to mend the terrace rail

effects.log: She is a quick pupil. By the autumn she is correcting you on knots, with her tongue out.

events.text: You tend the dark thing quietly, with a broom, a bucket, and an old rag. The village does not know what to make of you. A boy brings you water. An old man leaves a cup of rice wine on the wall each full moon, and takes the empty cup away at dawn, saying nothing. It is an exchange of silences, and you value it more than words.

choices.text: Pour a little of the wine on the ground, and sweep up after

effects.log: You do. The old man sees from his window and puts a second cup on the wall, the next moon.

choices.text: Thank the old man, in person, with a bow

effects.log: He is embarrassed. He mumbles something about the weather and shuffles off. The cup returns the next moon, full.

events.text: You tell them. In {llg_region}, the elders have their own way of testing a claimant, a quiet one: they bring out a worn wooden bowl and ask what was done with it at the evening meal. Nobody has answered yet. The bowl is chipped at the rim, in the shape of a thumb. The oldest man there says, "Tell us, then, if you were {llg_who}."

choices.text: Answer from the heart, in the plain way only you would

ok.log: You answer all three. The old man puts a trembling hand to his mouth. A hush falls like snow, and then someone sets down a cup.

fail.log: You answer, and falter on the last. They are kind about it, and the old man pats your arm, and the bowl goes back on its shelf.

choices.text: Show them the old skill, to prove the claim

ok.log: You show them. It is not a showy thing, and the villagers lean in. When you stop, nobody breathes.

fail.log: You show them, and the challenger at the door is quicker than the woodcut. The villagers murmur kindly. Your ribs ache.

choices.text: Laugh, and say it was only a story

effects.log: You laugh, and the elders look relieved. The wooden bowl is put away. It is probably the wisest way out.

events.text: You told them who you were, and the telling was met not with cheering but with a heavy kind of stillness. In {llg_region} they were taught to fear the name, and are being asked now to put a face to it. A woman at the back of the crowd is crying silently. A man near the front has taken off his hat and is turning it in his hands.

choices.text: Stay and let them look at you, as long as they need

effects.log: You stand through the long evening. When the last of them has gone, there is a lamp left lit on the wall.

choices.text: Offer to answer any question, however hard

effects.log: Questions come, halting at first. They are the hardest of your lives, and you answer each.

events.text: The archivist of the Jade Court's southern desk, a tall woman named Seo Ihwa with a nervous laugh, has been trying for years to clear up the entry for {llg_who}. She says the record is a tangle of contradictions, stuffed with legend. She hands you a pen and four sheets of corrections to check, and a plate of bean cakes. "Anything you can add," she says, "will be gratefully read."

choices.text: Correct the entry carefully, line by line

effects.log: It takes a week. At the end, Seo Ihwa reads the sheets and takes off her glasses. "Yes," she says, "that is the one that was missing."

choices.text: Add a footnote of your own, in a plain hand

effects.log: You write the footnote. Seo Ihwa cries a little, and then laughs at herself, and eats a bean cake.

events.text: You have written it all down, the full account, bad parts included, and the Jade Court sends a clerk to check it. The clerk, an unsmiling young man with fine handwriting, reads in the lamplight and says nothing for an hour. Then he asks, rather abruptly, whether you would like the true account to replace the old one in the archive, or be kept beside it.

choices.text: Replace the old entry, and let the truth stand alone

effects.log: The clerk makes a tidy note. In the spring, children learn the corrected dates, and the old errors fade like a bad dream.

choices.text: Keep it beside the old entry, so readers may compare

effects.log: The clerk sets the two side by side. A century on, scholars will argue over which came first, and be wrong.

events.text: The work goes on through the year, and the shrine slowly becomes a place one could live in. The carpenter, a gruff old fellow with a pipe, finally asks whose coin pays for the timber. You say it is a private matter. He grunts and strikes the next nail rather harder than he need. By midsummer the roof is on, and he is whistling.

choices.text: Pay for the last of the paint too

effects.log: The paint goes on in an afternoon. The carpenter steps back, sighing, with a look as if a favourite child had been washed.

choices.text: Leave the final nail for the carpenter to drive

effects.log: He drives it, slowly, with great ceremony. The whole village applauds, and he bows with the hammer.

events.text: A well is dug at the edge of the terrace in {llg_region}, paid by a patron who asks to be nameless. The crew are young and cheerful and sing while they work. When the water comes up, cold and clear, they throw a handful of it over each other and howl with joy. A child fills a gourd and drinks and says it tastes like mountains.

choices.text: Drink from the well with the crew

effects.log: The water is cold enough to ache. The crew shout and clap your back. You taste mountains too.

choices.text: Stand back and let them have the moment

effects.log: You watch the water-fight from the shade. It is the happiest sight you have seen in a month.

events.text: A small library is added to the shrine, a single room of cedar shelves for the village's papers, songs and old receipts, paid for anonymously. The first donor of books is a washerwoman, who brings a bundle of recipes tied with string. She is proud and terrified. The shelf is a bare plank. You help her place the bundle there, gently, among the dust.

choices.text: Help her label the shelf with the family name

effects.log: She spells it out, letter by letter. The brush shakes and the characters come out a little crooked, and perfect.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let her do it her own way

effects.log: She labels the shelf. It takes a long time. When she has finished she stands back, wiping her hands on her apron, and weeps.

events.text: You undo the thing piece by piece, in {llg_region}, over a hard year: the habits, the sealed rooms, the verses that no longer mean what they meant. People watch from windows. A woman brings you a bowl of soup and asks nothing. A man comes with a hammer and works beside you from dawn to noon without a word, then goes home to eat.

choices.text: Share the soup with the man at noon

effects.log: He accepts, wary at first, then hungry. You eat in silence on a pile of stones, and it is the first time you taste anything in weeks.

choices.text: Thank the woman, and ask whom the soup is really from

effects.log: She says it is from the whole street. You carry the empty bowl back with both hands, and a bowl of your own.

events.text: Tobeom arrives with Mirae in tow, and a surprising number of other people: three potters, a woman who sings to bees, and a boy with a goat. They have come, Mirae explains, to be useful. Tobeom surveys {llg_thing} and says, "Well. Somebody has let it get tidy." She seems to mean it as an accusation. By evening everyone is covered in plaster, and fed.

choices.text: Join the plastering and learn from the potters

effects.log: The potters laugh at your plaster and show you how it is done. You go to bed sticky and glad.

choices.text: Feed the whole crew from your own larder

effects.log: The goat gets the best of it. Tobeom grunts her approval, which is an honour, and eats three helpings.

events.text: A cloud-barge bringing visitors to {llg_thing} arrives with a tall, eager man in the lead. He is a restorer from the capital isle, with a portfolio of drawings and a plan to "bring it back to its original glory." Tobeom looks at his drawings for an hour, says nothing, and offers him tea. Mirae mutters, behind a pot, that this is the most dangerous thing Tobeom does.

choices.text: Ask him to show you the original glory he has in mind

effects.log: He unrolls a drawing with a flourish. It is lovely, and entirely invented. Tobeom's tea is poured, with a smile like a drawn blade.

choices.text: Offer to take him up the scaffold and let him see the real beams

effects.log: He goes, surprised. By the top he is quiet. By the bottom he is asking where to start.

events.text: A new patron, a stern grey-haired woman in travelling silks, comes to {llg_thing} to see how her donation was spent. She finds Tobeom asleep on a bench, Mirae painting a gutter, and you in the middle of a heap of tiles. The patron says nothing for a long time. Then she asks, with great gravity, whether the roof will hold through the monsoon.

choices.text: Tell her honestly that the roof will need another year

effects.log: The patron nods, unsurprised. "Then I will come again next year," she says, and leaves a purse of stones on the bench.

choices.text: Tell her the roof will hold, and offer to prove it on the ladder

ok.log: You take her up the ladder. She climbs like a cat, stamps on the tiles, and is satisfied. Tobeom wakes and says "Told you."

fail.log: You take her up the ladder, and a tile slides under her boot with a clatter. She laughs, then frowns, then hires a roofer on the spot.

events.text: A ferrywoman of the Rho family, Danbi's cousin, brings a small clay jar to your door on the day of the recitation. Inside is a paper strip with the first name on the family account, written in a child's hand, very old. She says it has been copied out by every generation, and that tradition says it must be handed to the one who sits at the end of the list. She sets it in your palm.

choices.text: Read the name aloud, and keep the strip

effects.log: You read it. Your voice is not what you expected. The ferrywoman bows, and you hear her cry a little on the stair as she goes.

choices.text: Ask her what the family hopes you will do with it

effects.log: She thinks hard, at length. "Not forget," she says at last, and wipes her eyes, and goes.

events.text: Late in life you have become a kind of local fixture at {llg_thing}, like the lantern at the gate. Visitors greet you before they greet the abbot. A young priest brings you tea at noon and has never once asked who you were. Today he asks, rather shyly, what it is like to be so fond of a place. You find that you can answer, and that the answer is short.

choices.text: Tell him it is like being a guest who is never asked to leave

effects.log: He laughs, then looks thoughtful. He pours you a second cup and sits on the step beside you.

choices.text: Tell him it is like coming home to a house that was kept for you

effects.log: He is quiet for a moment. "It is," he says, "and I think I understand now," and takes the cup away gently.

events.text: Years on, you hear that the old place has a festival now, with paper boats and a lantern parade, and that a child dressed as the founder wins the costume prize every year. You are too far away to attend. You send a basket of persimmons instead, unsigned, and the festival eats them with great delight and no idea at all.

choices.text: Imagine the parade, and raise a small cup of tea to it

effects.log: You raise the cup toward the east. The wind carries a thread of drum-beats, probably imagined.

choices.text: Write the festival a one-line letter of thanks, and burn it

effects.log: The smoke goes up. You feel, absurdly, that it has been read.

events.text: The steward of {ct4_house} calls on you with a tray of small gifts: a jade comb, a cup of old plum wine, a cousin's hand in marriage. {bh4_kin} is the cousin, and stands shyly behind him. Each gift has a string, and each string runs through the steward's fingers. "The house only wishes you to be happy here," he says, and means that you are to stay.

choices.text: Accept the match and the gifts

effects.log: You accept, one by one. The steward's fingers close on the strings. The cousin smiles shyly, and the comb is very beautiful.

choices.text: Return every gift, with courtesy

effects.log: You return them in the order they were given. The steward's smile does not change. His fingers let the strings drop one by one.

events.text: A long letter from the head of {ct4_house} arrives, scented with sandalwood. It says you have been a joy to the house, that the seat of {bh4_cap} would sit well on your shoulders, and that a guest so loved should not be exposed to the winds of the wider isles. It is the kindest cage you have ever read. {bh4_kin} has pinned a flower to the seal.

choices.text: Reply with thanks, and accept the seat

effects.log: Your reply is warm. The seat is a fine one, and the flower on the seal wilts as you write.

choices.text: Reply with thanks, and keep your freedom of the road

effects.log: Your reply is warm and firm. The head's answer comes a week later, three lines long, and cooler by a degree.

events.text: The festival of {ct4_house} honours you with a place at the high table, a robe of the house colours, and a new name, "Friend of the Line." The robe is soft. The name is loud. Across the table {bh4_kin} lifts a cup to you with a smile that wants something. Every eye in the hall has been fitted with the thought that you are theirs now.

choices.text: Wear the robe, and answer to the new name

effects.log: The robe fits perfectly. The hall applauds. Somewhere inside you, a small door closes, politely.

choices.text: Thank them, and ask to keep your own name

effects.log: The hall goes quiet for a breath, then decides to find it charming. The robe is folded into a box and left at your door.

events.text: Each day a small kindness arrives at your pavilion from {ct4_house}: a basket of peaches, a repaired roof-tile, a message of regard. Each is an anchor, a very light one. {bh4_kin} comes in person today with the most delicate: a promise of a lifetime seat, written on silk, waiting only for your thumbprint.

choices.text: Press your thumb to the silk

effects.log: The thumbprint is a perfect oval. {bh4_kin} thanks you in a voice so grateful it is almost frightening.

choices.text: Hand the silk back, and thank {bh4_kin} for the thought

effects.log: You hand it back. The house's kindnesses do not cease, but they come slower, and with less sugar.

events.text: You discover that your pavilion's lease has been quietly paid for the next hundred years by {ct4_house}. Nobody asked you. Nobody told you. {bh4_kin} comes by to mention that it was only a small thing, between friends, and sits to drink your tea, with the air of a person who has just handed over a deed and a leash.

choices.text: Accept the gift with gratitude, and let the lease stand

effects.log: The tea is poured. {bh4_kin} leans back, satisfied. The pavilion seems a little smaller, and more comfortable.

choices.text: Insist on repaying the lease, in your own coin

effects.log: You send the payment by courier. The house refuses it twice, then accepts, with a tone you can feel through the paper.

events.text: The house has stopped smiling at you, and begun to write. A notice is pinned to the door of your pavilion: your seat at the long table has been reassigned "pending review." A steward collects your teacups for inventory. {ct4_house} has the manners of a great line, so none of this is rude. All of it is a door being closed, one hinge at a time.

choices.text: Go to the table, sit in your seat, and wait

effects.log: You sit. The room gets quiet in the old way. The review, when it comes, finds an awkward truth in your favour.

choices.text: Pack the teacups yourself and leave before they finish

effects.log: You pack with care, and the steward watches, mortified. You are on the cloud-road by evening, light and unfollowed.

events.text: A rumour has been put into the corridors of {ct4_house}: that you kept something from the last accounting, or took something from the last feast. It has been told so well that three people have apologised to you in advance. {bh4_kin} no longer meets your eye. A date has been set for a hearing, and the hall for it has been scrubbed already.

choices.text: Appear at the hearing, and answer every charge

effects.log: You answer. It takes the whole day and most of your temper. By dusk the rumour has the thin, ill look of a thing found out.

choices.text: Send your regrets, and take the cloud-road before the date

effects.log: The date comes and goes without you. The rumour, left to itself, grows larger, and you are glad to be a long way from it.

events.text: The elders of {ct4_house} gather at the foot of your stair at dusk with lanterns, in a courteous half-ring, and tell you that your presence has become "a disquiet." None of them is unkind. All of them have been told what to say. {bh4_kin} stands among them, looking at the sky. You are being asked to explain why a guest should stay.

choices.text: Answer them, calmly, and say you will remain

effects.log: You speak for a quarter-hour. When you stop, the lanterns are still. After a time, one by one, the elders go home.

choices.text: Thank them, and say you will go in the morning

effects.log: They bow. A few look relieved, a few look ashamed. At dawn the stair is empty and your pavilion is dewy and quiet.

events.text: In the night your pavilion's cranes are let out, one by one, and flown to far isles. Your tea-service is found in pieces on the stair. A note under your door says, in a clerk's hand, that the guest-fund is closed to you. {ct4_house} does not shout. It simply removes the things that make a place a home, and watches to see what you do.

choices.text: Stay, and rebuild with your own hands

effects.log: You gather the pieces. By the end of the week the pavilion is livelier than before, and half the house has found reasons to visit.

choices.text: Take what is left and leave by the cloud-road

effects.log: You take the pieces that matter. The cranes, you hear later, come home to you of their own accord, one by one.

events.text: At the spring banquet of {ct4_house} a young scion proposes a toast to "the finest guest the house has ever had." It is meant as praise and lands as a label. He adds that of course the seat of {bh4_cap} is the very highest a friend may reach, and the table nods. {bh4_kin} does not nod. {bh4_kin} looks at you.

choices.text: Raise a cup to the toast, and smile without comment

effects.log: The table relaxes. Only {bh4_kin} sees the corner of your mouth, and files it away.

choices.text: Thank him, and ask what the seat above it is called

effects.log: The table goes still. The scion laughs, a little shrill. {bh4_kin} hides a smile in a cup.

events.text: An old aunt of {ct4_house}, beloved and half deaf, asks you at the top of her voice whether it is true that you are "not from here." The hall hears. She then tells everyone, at the same volume, that this is no shame, that it has been done before, and that {bh4_cap} is a lovely thing to be. She pats your hand. She is a genuinely kind woman, and it is a terrible moment.

choices.text: Thank the aunt warmly, and let the laughter pass

effects.log: You are warm. She beams. The hall laughs gently, and for once the laugh is on all of you.

choices.text: Tell her plainly that you are not from here, and that you like it

effects.log: The hall is startled. The aunt nods, delighted. {bh4_kin} lowers a cup, slowly, and looks at you in a new way.

events.text: A lantern is hung over your seat at the festival of {ct4_house}, white where the others are red. It is a courtesy, the steward whispers: the colour of honoured guests. It is also a signal visible from every corner of the hall. {bh4_kin} adjusts the lantern with a kindly hand, and says it suits you.

choices.text: Sit beneath the white lantern with good grace

effects.log: You sit. The white light is soft and rather unflattering. Guests look and look away, and by midnight nobody notices it at all.

choices.text: Ask for a red lantern, to match the rest

effects.log: There is a pause that stretches. A red lantern is brought, and hung beside the white. For a time the hall can talk of nothing else.

events.text: The family genealogist of {ct4_house} is showing visitors the great scroll of the line, and halts at the end where a margin has been left, blank, for guests. "We keep a little room," she says kindly, "for those of other blood." The visitors coo. {bh4_kin} is standing next to you, very still, and says nothing, which is a kind of speech.

choices.text: Look at the margin and say it is a handsome piece of work

effects.log: The genealogist glows. The visitors move on. {bh4_kin} lets out a breath, and lingers a moment at your side.

choices.text: Ask whether anyone has ever been moved from the margin into the line

effects.log: The genealogist considers for a long moment. "Once," she says. "It caused a great deal of trouble." The visitors have gone very silent.

events.text: Children of {ct4_house} play a game in the court where one is the Guest and the rest are the House, and the Guest must try to reach a painted stool while the House blocks. The Guest is allowed to reach {bh4_cap} and no further, and the stool is painted accordingly. They invite you to play, as an honour. {bh4_kin} watches from the gallery, unreadable.

choices.text: Play the Guest, and lose with good humour

effects.log: You are blocked by a seven-year-old with unshakable aim. The court roars. {bh4_kin} laughs aloud, once, and covers it with a hand.

choices.text: Play the Guest, and run round the whole court to the real stool

effects.log: The children shriek and chase. The painted stool is toppled. The gallery, startled, begins to clap.

events.text: The disciples of {bb_house} file onto the practice terrace at dusk, and you speak to them one last time of the {bb_art}. It is for these walls and no others, you say. A girl of twelve asks, very reasonably, what happens if a wall falls down. There is a silence full of cranes. A boy snickers and is hushed. You find you have not prepared for the question.

choices.text: Answer the girl honestly, and let the silence settle

effects.log: You tell her the art goes where the people go, and that is exactly the problem. She nods slowly, like a very small elder.

choices.text: Tell the whole terrace why the art must stay

effects.log: You speak for a quarter-hour, plainly. The terrace is quiet. In the dusk, a few of them are already practising the stance, softly, with their hands.

events.text: You summon the heads of the nine branches of {bb_house} to the ancestral hall and read out the binding on the {bb_art}, line by line. Three branches approve at once. Four want more. Two look as if they have been struck. The oldest, a woman of great age, sits with her hands on her cane and says, "I was against this the first time, and I am against it now." She stays seated.

choices.text: Hear her out, and honour her objection in the record

effects.log: You write her objection into the margin. She nods, as if closing a door softly. The hall relaxes by a hair.

choices.text: Press the binding to the vote, and let the branches decide

effects.log: It passes by a thin count. The old woman rises on her cane and leaves without a word. The hall rings with it for days.

events.text: The great line of {bb_house} holds a night-vigil for the binding of the {bb_art}, with cousins from every cloud-chain in attendance. A chain of paper lanterns is strung from tablet to tablet, and every guest lights one. By custom, anyone who disagrees may blow theirs out. At midnight, one lantern goes dark at the far end of the hall. Everyone pretends not to see.

choices.text: Walk down the hall and stand by the dark lantern

effects.log: You stand beside it, saying nothing. After a time its owner relights it, and nods. The hall exhales.

choices.text: Leave the dark lantern alone, and keep the vigil to dawn

effects.log: You keep the vigil. At dawn, the dark lantern is still dark. Nobody speaks of it again, and nobody forgets.

events.text: A scroll nailed to the refectory door of {bb_house} proclaims that the {bb_art} is the blood's, and nobody else's, from this morning onward. The disciples read it over their congee in a murmur. You know the {bb_art}. Someone at the next table spills his tea. An old gardener, at the end of the bench, goes on eating, steadily, with a face of weathered stone.

choices.text: Finish your congee and say nothing

effects.log: You finish. The gardener glances at you once, a quick approving look, and returns to his bowl.

choices.text: Ask the gardener what the scroll will cost the house

effects.log: He sets down his spoon. "More than it saves," he says, softly, and picks the spoon up again.

events.text: A young attendant of the guest pavilion in {bb_house} knocks at your door with a tray of tea and an expression of distressed duty. She has been sent, she explains, to tell you the {bb_art} is now bound to the blood, and that you are not to teach it. You know it. She knows you know it. Her hands tremble on the tray, and the tea sloshes a little.

choices.text: Take the tray steady in your hands, and thank her kindly

effects.log: She almost weeps with relief. You drink the tea together, standing, in silence, and it is the best you have had in a year.

choices.text: Ask her to carry back a question to the steward

effects.log: She nods, flustered. The question is courteous and pointed, and the steward's answer, three days later, is neither.

events.text: {npc} finds you at the cloud-ferry landing in the grey of early morning, wearing a plain robe and holding a lantern. "I will be brief," {he} says. "The {bb_art} was seen again, in your hands, by a trader from the western isles. {bb_house} heard of it within a week. They would like you to stop." {He} says it kindly. That makes it worse.

choices.text: Promise to stop, and mean it

effects.log: You promise. {npc} nods and lowers the lantern. The ferry arrives, and neither of you boards it for a while.

choices.text: Say that {he} may try to make you stop

ok.log: You rise and step onto the landing-stones. {npc} sets the lantern down with great care and takes up a stance you know.

fail.log: You step out, and {npc} steps in. You hit the stones before the lantern stops swinging. {He} picks it up and goes.

choices.text: Offer the house a price for the right to keep it

effects.log: You name a sum. {npc} writes it on a small slip and tucks it away. "It may be enough," {he} says. "It may not."

events.text: A knock at your gate at midday, and {npc} stands outside with a basket of persimmons from the house orchard. "A gift," {he} says. "And a word." The word, delivered over tea, is that the {bb_art} is the blood's of {bb_house}, and that you, who left, have been seen using it. The persimmons, {he} adds, are very good this year.

choices.text: Give your word to put it away

effects.log: You give it. {npc} peels a persimmon and offers you half, as people do who have agreed on a thing.

choices.text: Say the house may try to take it from you

ok.log: You rise. {npc} sets down the persimmon with a sigh. The tea goes cold on the table.

fail.log: You rise, and {npc} sets down the persimmon, and in a moment you are looking at the ceiling. {He} finishes the persimmon before leaving.

choices.text: Ask what it would take for the house to look the other way

effects.log: You are told, precisely. {npc} has the figure ready, written on the inside of a sleeve.

events.text: On a quiet evening {npc} is waiting in your garden, seated on the stone bench beneath the plum tree, hands folded. "I did not want to come," {he} says. "They sent me because I know you." The {bb_art} was used at the autumn market in front of two hundred witnesses, and {bb_house} has had a hard month of letters. {He} looks tired.

choices.text: Promise it will not be used in public again

effects.log: You promise. {npc} unfolds {his} hands, slowly, and lets out a breath that seems to come from far away.

choices.text: Say that if the house wants it back, it should send someone willing to try

ok.log: You say it, regretting how it sounds. {npc} stands, and you both step onto the gravel.

fail.log: You step onto the gravel and are on your back before you hear {npc} move. {He} apologises, sincerely, and helps you up.

choices.text: Offer to pay the house for the art you carry

effects.log: You name a sum, and {npc} frowns. "They will want to be asked nicely," {he} says. "They will want it in writing."

events.text: {npc} arrives at your gate with a staff and a clean white sash, the old sign of a formal reckoning. "No more letters," {he} says. "You were asked three times to put away the {bb_art}, and you did not. I am here to ask a fourth, with the staff." The neighbours have gathered on their balconies. A child waves.

choices.text: Take up your own staff and answer

ok.log: You take it from the rack. The neighbours fall silent. {npc} bows, you bow, and the court is very still.

fail.log: You take up the staff and are disarmed in three exchanges. {npc} sets the staff against the wall, and says the fourth question is answered.

choices.text: Put the art away, and say so aloud

effects.log: You say it where the neighbours can hear. {npc} lowers the staff. The child, on the balcony, stops waving.

events.text: You come home to find {npc} sitting very straight on your veranda, a pot of tea half drunk beside {him}, and a folded paper under the pot. The paper is the final notice from {bb_house}. "I have waited since noon," {he} says. "I am willing to go on waiting, or to settle it now. The house would prefer the second."

choices.text: Settle it now, in the courtyard

ok.log: You step down. {npc} sets down the cup and follows. The courtyard is raked and quiet, and the first move is made without a word.

fail.log: You step down, and the courtyard is quiet, and the match is short. {npc} helps you up and refills your tea.

choices.text: Ask for the house's price, and pay it

effects.log: The price is written on the inside of the notice. You read it twice. {npc} pretends to study the plum tree while you decide.

events.text: A courier-crane lands on your rail at dawn with a scroll tied to its leg. The scroll is brief: {npc} will come at noon, alone, for the last time, to ask about the {bb_art}. A small drawing of a tea-cup is added at the bottom, in {his} hand, a joke between old acquaintances. At noon there is a knock at your gate.

choices.text: Open the gate, tea ready, and meet {him} in the yard

ok.log: You open it. The yard is swept. {npc} comes in, and in the end it is a good, hard match.

fail.log: You open the gate, and the match is a good, hard one, and {npc} wins. {He} accepts your tea afterwards, which is a courtesy.

choices.text: Open the gate and promise to put the art away

effects.log: You promise before the gate is fully open. {npc} bows, and leaves the cup of tea you offered untouched, which is also a courtesy.

events.text: A lantern left on your windowsill, unlit, and under it a note in {npc}'s hand. It does not say goodbye. It says the {bb_art} is too good to be kept in a jar, and that {he} wants to see what it looks like in a wider room. By the time you read it, the ferry-bell has rung twice, and the elders of {bb_house} are at the door.

choices.text: Set your people to follow and bring them back

effects.log: You give the order from the doorway. The elders nod, grimly pleased. You close the door and hear your own heart.

choices.text: Go after them yourself

ok.log: You find {npc} at the third landing, sitting on a crate, looking suddenly very young. You talk until dusk. {He} comes home with you.

fail.log: You find {npc} at the third landing. {He} hears all of it, thanks you gravely, and boards the ferry anyway.

choices.text: Let them go, and strike the binding from the register

effects.log: You say it in the doorway. The elders argue for a month. In the meantime {npc} is already somewhere under a different roof, and free.

events.text: A page torn from a ledger comes to you in the beak of a messenger-bird, in the hand of a clerk of the western ferries. It records that a young passenger paid for passage in the form of the {bb_art}, which the ferry-hands had asked to see. The signature is {npc}'s. The elders of {bb_house} have also seen the page. They are waiting at your door, politely.

choices.text: Send your people to bring {him} back

effects.log: You give the order with your sleeve over your mouth. The elders go away satisfied. The page is burned.

choices.text: Follow the ferry yourself

ok.log: You catch up with {npc} at the next landing. {He} listens and weeps and returns with you, a day late and very quiet.

fail.log: You catch up with {npc} at the next landing, and {he} listens, and weeps, and boards the ferry anyway. You watch it go.

choices.text: Let {him} go, and lift the binding

effects.log: You fold the page and give it to the elders as a receipt. Next morning you strike the line from the register, and the house changes colour slightly.

events.text: A caravan-master selling tea at the landing tells you, over the price of leaves, about a young stranger who won every bout at the lower-isles fair with a style no one had seen: unbroken, fluid, an art the local masters called "the house in a jar." It is the {bb_art}. It is {npc}. The caravan-master looks pleased to have been of use.

choices.text: Send your people to find them and bring them home

effects.log: You buy the tea, thank the seller, and send for the ones whose business this is. The caravan-master is paid in full.

choices.text: Go after them yourself

ok.log: You find {npc} on a lower isle, hoarse from laughing, surrounded by admirers. {He} sees you, and the laughter stops. You walk home together at dusk.

fail.log: You find {npc} on a lower isle, surrounded by admirers. {He} sees you, shakes {his} head with a small smile, and does not leave.

choices.text: Let them go, and lift the binding

effects.log: You tip the caravan-master well and say nothing to the elders. That evening you strike the line from the register in your own hand.

events.text: A pair of old stewards of the Ancestral Hall have walked the whole way from the home isle, because a letter would have been disrespectful. They sit stiffly on your veranda and say that the head of the house has asked, in confidence, for you to take the seal. The line is thin, they say. The ledgers are thick. They can wait a season, no longer, for an answer.

choices.text: Accept the seal, and the weight of it

effects.log: You say yes. The stewards rise, bow, and begin at once to tell you what is wrong. You listen to all of it, and some of it is worse than you thought.

choices.text: Decline, and let the head keep the seat

effects.log: They nod, unsurprised, and drink their tea, and look at your garden a long time. They will come again in a hundred years, if any of you are still there.

events.text: The invitation comes at the new moon, on silk the colour of a very old bruise. The head of your blood is ready to step down. The elders have counted the votes, twice, and your name is on both counts. The letter ends without a plea, which is how you know it is a serious one. Your hand, as you read, is warmer than it should be.

choices.text: Answer yes, and fly home to take the seat

effects.log: You send the answer by dawn. The flight home takes three days, and on the third you begin to understand what you have agreed to.

choices.text: Answer no, with respect, and with a gift

effects.log: You send the answer with a fine bolt of cloud-silk. The elders accept the gift, and write again in a century, with the same silk and a longer letter.
